subsubtopic: QUEBEC WHITE PAPER ON LANGUAGE POLICY-FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN DISCUSSION AND ACTION TO PROTECT MINORITY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. It concerns the White Paper on language policy which was tabled by the government of Quebec in the national assembly of that province on Friday, a paper which challenges the spirit of the Official Languages Act and possibly contains some conflict of constitutional guarantees relating to minority rights. Since this paper was tabled as a discussion paper, I wonder if the Prime Minister could advise the House whether the government of Canada intends
April 4, 1977

to become formally involved in the discussion, at least through a statement in this House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: QUEBEC WHITE PAPER ON LANGUAGE POLICY-FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN DISCUSSION AND ACTION TO PROTECT MINORITY RIGHTS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. We have not contemplated that. I would gladly answer any questions on the subject. I am sure my ministers will feel free to comment on it as it might affect the rights of citizens of Quebec. We do, however, consider it to be a white paper, not legislation as of yet. We very much hope that that white paper will change in some important aspects before it is made into law. I agree completely with the Leader of the Opposition when he says it challenges in some aspects the spirit of the Official Languages Act. I think he would recognize with me that the aim of the white paper in so far as it is to establish a regional culture in Quebec is one which all of us can support. Indeed, it is an aim which the federal government has been pursuing through many of its cultural institufions such as the CBC, the National Film Board, the Official Languages Act and so on. Beyond establishing this culture, it seems to take steps that are regressive rather than progressive. We hope that the citizens of Quebec in particular will prefer an open society where the minority rights are absolutely respected, rather than go back toward a unilingual Quebec and perhaps a unilingual English Canada which is a state to which we do not want to return.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC WHITE PAPER ON LANGUAGE POLICY-FEDERAL PARTICIPATION IN DISCUSSION AND ACTION TO PROTECT MINORITY RIGHTS

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: BRUCELLOSIS-POSSIBILITY OF RETURNING TO VACCINATION PROGRAM
speechtext: What we are doing in that area is rechecking to make sure we have covered all the herds, to make sure they are free of the disease. Up to now, 75 per cent of the herds have been tested. speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the House at this time of the main features of the 1977-78 dairy program which has been worked out in consultation with the nine provinces represented on the Canadian milk supply management committee and the Canadian Dairy Commission.
Effective April 1, 1977, there is an increase in the target returns level from $11.45 to $11.86 per hundredweight on industrial milk testing at 3.5 per cent butterfat. This increase is in line with the formula identified in the long-term dairy policy which allows returns to keep pace with increased production costs. Producers will have higher net returns this dairy year because target returns are higher and the in-quota levy is lower. Net returns for this dairy year are estimated at $10.66 per hundredweight compared with $10.10 last year. The increase in farmer returns comes from raising the support price for butter by 10 cents to $1.18 per pound, and by increasing skim milk powder from 68 cents per pound to 70 cents. The federal subsidy payment on industrial milk remains unchanged at $2.66 per hundredweight. It will be paid on all industrial milk shipments up to 100 million hundredweights which is the total production estimated to fill the national requirement.
Total market share quota for Canada is established at 105.6 million hundredweights for the year. This total allows for a 5 per cent sleeve over the 100 million hundredweights projected as the national requirement, and allows for a small protected

quota expansion in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
The government will be taking over the current total debt of $152 million of the export equalization fund which was introduced in 1975 to help the Canadian dairy industry cope with increased export losses due to weakening world markets. With the write-off of the fund, industrial milk producers will be paying 15 cents less per hundredweight on in-quota shipments of industrial milk. The in-quota levy this year is set at $1.20 per hundredweight, and the over-quota levy has been reduced to $7 per hundredweight from $8.60.
Fluid milk shippers will be expected to share some portion of the costs associated with the export of surplus skim milk powder. The cheese import quota will remain unchanged from last year at 50 million pounds. The government is allocating $20 million to the Canadian Dairy Commission for handling storage and marketing costs. The $20 million allocated last year to the Canadian International Development Agency to purchase skim milk powder for food aid will remain unchanged, and the government will be spending an additional $4 million on market research to find new uses and markets for this product in Canada.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that there is a debate of some importance before this House today. I would like, therefore, to close by commenting on the substantial reduction that has been made in the surplus stocks held by the Canadian Dairy Commission. The Dairy Commission at this time has approximately 10 million pounds of butter and some 52 million pounds of skim milk powder unsold. With this reduction, and with continuing attention being paid to controlled, even annual milk supply, I am confident that the Canadian dairy industry is in a far stronger position that it has been for some time and that it can, as far as I am concerned, look forward with confidence to the future.

Seventy-one per cent of all commercial farms in Quebec are dairy farms. 1 think I do. I am convinced that the minister will never forget certain events associated with his bad judgment and bad decisions this past year. This statement increases the target price from $11.45 to $11.86 per hundredweight. It should be noted that the producers do not receive that target price. Excluding any penalty, but taking into account haulage, export levies, licence fees, and advertising, the amount actually received by producers would be approximately $3 less. Thus, the return of $9.86 per hundredweight would be realized, consequently less than the estimate by the minister of $10.66.
Production costs do vary, but well documented studies indicate a figure in the neighbourhood of $14 a hundredweight. In many cases producers are subsidizing their own product to the extent of $3 per hundredweight. An in-depth study has revealed that in many cases milk sales alone do not provide sufficient income to cover the freight: the milk cheque income must be supplemented by sales of breeding stock, sales of cash crops and, in many cases, off-the-farm jobs. The real sleeper in this statement is the sentence which reads:
Fluid milk producers will be expected to share some portion of the costs associated with the export of surplus skim milk powder.
It is said that the financial requirements for export losses are $140 million. If they are not, then I am suggesting that the Canadian Dairy Commission has been hoodwinking the respective milk marketing agencies across this country. If they are at $140 million, and if the levy on industrial milk is $1.25 per hundredweight, which by my calcultions would provide $112.8 million, then the shortfall would be $27.2 million. This would mean a levy on fluid production of approximately 23 cents to 25 cents per hundredweight. It is obvious that the provinces do not want a levy on their fluid production. Ontario fluid producers would be asked to contribute $11 million, Quebec fluid producers would be required to contribute $6,5 million, and all other provinces accordingly. This matter must be clarified and the minister should be severely chastised for not clarifying this item in his statement today.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) today goes a long way in clearing up some of the difficulties that he got himself into during the last two years. It is a policy that he is scurrying on because of the mountain of powdered milk that is left over as a surplus because of the dairy policies of the last two years. Dairy farmers need more quotas. There is an increase in the quotas of 5 per cent. That will help a bit, but I suggest it will not help enough.
The other positive thing I see in the policy announced by the minister today is that the government is absorbing a loss on the export of skim milk powder to the tune of some $152 million. There is another positive note in the policy announced by the minister, and that is the anticipated or estimated increase in net income of dairy farmers or industrial milk producers in this country. The estimated increase is 56 cents per hundredweight. That is small, but I suggest it is welcome after two years of declining income because of the unco-ordinated policy approach the government has taken.
I want to make three or four more points that I think the government and the minister should be thinking of in the long term. Surely to goodness we need in this country a lot more long-term planning for both producers and consumers. We must do something about the surplus of skim milk powder that we have in this country, on a long-term basis. So far we have seen short-term compromise policies. 1 suggest that is really not good enough.
The Canadian International Development Agency is purchasing skim milk powder at less than the cost of production of skim milk powder to the dairy producers. That has to be changed. It is a problem we have to resolve. It is a serious problem not only here but in the European Economic Community and elsewhere where there are very many dairy farms.
The time has come in this country where we should have a national school milk program. I make that point emphatically. The minister has said several times that he endorses that program in principle. That is fine, but somebody has to pay for it. The federal government should enter into a program with the provinces where they pay 50 per cent of the cost of putting milk into the schools of this nation. There are precedents for that in many of the social schemes and health schemes that we have in Canada. Surely to goodness people of this country need to drink more milk. From the point of view of nutrition, they have to drink more milk and eat more dairy products. One way of doing that is by starting early, when people are young, throughout the school system.
If you had a school milk program, and if you had the Coke machines and Pepsi machines thrown out of the schools, perhaps you would change some of the nutritional habits, of young people in this country and at the same time assist dairy

farmers in terms of having a more guaranteed, stable and secure income.
The other thing that has to be done, according to the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), is to reduce cheese imports. For the second year in a row there has been a freeze on the amount of cheese imports-I think 50 million pounds. I suggest very strongly to the minister that he reduce those imports so that Canadians eat more Canadian cheese. I know people who want to start producing cheese in this country. They are having difficulty because of the lack of imaginative programs by federal and provincial governments, and competition as a result of imported cheese. The government should clarify its earlier position that 10 per cent of Canadian dairy products marketed be filled by imports. If we have the ability and potential to be self-sufficient in any aspect of the food industry, we should have a goal of feeding ourselves and, in turn, being self-sufficient.
One could say a number of other things about the dairy policy, but those are the salient points that come to my mind and to the minds of most dairy farmers in this country. It is important that we keep in mind that we need long-term planning so that dairy farmers can have increased quotas and a secure income. We should look closely at the school milk program, resolving the problem of skim milk powder in this country and reducing the amount of cheese that we import.

On the other hand, I regret the fact that the government was not able to abolish totally the levy on over-quota deliveries. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has made several comments with regard to fluid milk producers as if they did not contribute anything to the industrial surplus that we were confronted with, and the levy on industrial milk producers. The fact is that in the year 1974-75 there was an increase of 9 per cent in total milk produced by fluid milk producers. Coupled with a decline of 1 per cent in class 1 sales, the result has been an increase of 41 per cent in industrial milk produced by fluid milk producers. Compare that 41 per cent with the 7.3 per cent in the shipment of industrial milk produced in 1974-75.
I could go on and give all kinds of figures to show that the producers have benefited from this program but have not contributed very much. We are asking them to contribute 25 cents per hundredweight. There are only two other avenues I have. If they do not go along with this program, we will work out a percentage of the subsidy we pay them for the surplus that they put into the industrial milk program. It would be much more costly for them to do it that way. Also, the provinces can pay us a grant in lieu of that levy. They can take it out of the treasury of the province.
Butterfat competes in the industrial milk market. We can use it as an example. For instance, last year butter could be brought to this country at about 35 cents a pound. If the fluid milk producer had sold his butterfat skim-off at that rate, you can imagine what it would have cost him. For them to say that they are not involved in this over-all picture is wrong. That shortfall has to be made up. I gather from the figures quoted by the hon. member that he is referring to the total amount of milk, including the sleeve. I was not talking about the sleeve. We are right on target this year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the budget of last Thursday has been described as a stand-pat budget; that is, stand pat with more unemployment than last year, and stand pat with less real growth. To call that a stand-pat situation is a bit like General Custer claiming that he stood pat at the battle of Little Bighorn, his last stand. Some day, and I would suggest that today is as good a day as any, this House and this country must start to wake up. Our economy is in serious difficulty. Such irreparable harm has been done in the past six years that we are now faced with a crisis to which few in this country appear to be willing to address themselves. Certainly, this government likes to befog the issue. If the Prime Minister of this country had been president or chief executive officer of a responsible Canadian business corporation, he would have been fired in 1972.

speechtext:
Sir, the minister's national accounts deficit for this year is up by 90 per cent over what he anticipated last year. Unemployment is higher, real growth is lower while inflation remains higher, and our trade remains in imbalance. We find that the current account deficit for this country in the last two years has been greater than the combined deficits of the United States, Germany, France, Japan, Great Britain and Italy. The administration has taken five years getting us into

this mess and it is time they gave us some indication of what the next five years will hold for us, if they remain in power.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: More inflation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the course of my remarks I shall touch upon some aspects of the budget which was tabled last Thursday. My colleague from Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) will speak in more detail on youth unemployment. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) will speak on labour matters generally and the government's unsatisfactory handling of labour: The hon. members for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) and Joliette (Mr. La Salle) will speak on regional disparities, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) will deal with urban affairs, housing, business and related matters, and the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) will speak on our country's lack of research and development.
Speaking generally, the federal government has three main tasks with respect to the economy. First, it must ensure that governmental activities are run soundly and efficiently, with the least possible taxation and minimum deficit financing. Second, the government must cultivate an economic climate which will provide full employment for those wishing to work, with a minimum of inflation. To do this it is necessary to inspire confidence in the private sector, which in turn ensures a co-operative and positive attitude as between business and labour. Third, since Canada depends heavily on world trade it is essential for our federal government to structure our activities in a way which will ensure that we remain competitive and able to maintain our position as a trading nation. Those three functions of government are interrelated. If the government is irresponsible in the discharging of its first function, that, in turn, influences the nation's performance with respect to employment, the containing of inflation and the maintaining of our position as a world trader.
This government, sir, has failed in all three respects in the past five years. The magnitude of their failure is not being dramatized. Let us review the facts. Personal income taxation of the average family in Canada has jumped so that today it is a bigger expense for Canadian families than any other single item. It costs the average family more than it spends on housing or food and much more than it spends on transportation. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first assumed power it was not so. Today the average Canadian family spends almost 20 per cent of its income on personal income tax. In the United States that figure is 14 per cent. That difference in taxation is the result of Canadian government's now taking 43 per cent of our gross national product, compared to 35 per cent in the United States.
That dead load in extra government costs, 8 per cent of our gross national product, or in dollar terms about $1,300 per taxpayer, puts a pressure on our productive people that is not shared by their counterparts in the United States. Bearing that added load, our workers demand higher wages to offset the
April 4, 1977

added tax load being imposed by government. It is the take-home pay workers are interested in. If they are taxed more, naturally they will demand that their gross wages go up. And if you not only tax them more but charge them twice the amount for unemployment insurance premiums charged in the United States, is it any wonder our workers demand higher wages than are being paid at present in the United States? In short, it is government greed and lack of responsibility which has contributed to our present plight more than any other single factor in the country.
This greed is shown at the Ottawa level in two ways. First, in the six years ended last October, federal spending jumped 151 per cent, almost twice as fast as the general increase in our economy. Second, since 1971 the government's take of our gross national product has risen from 38 per cent to 43 per cent; and of that 5 per cent increase, 80 per cent has taken place at the federal government level. We have touched on the taxation which has resulted from this federal governments spending spree. We have not touched, however, on the deficits and debt that has been and will be incurred in Ottawa.
Last Thursday's budget reveals that this government intends to run a budgetary deficit this year of $7.2 billion. This deficit is greater than total federal spending for the fiscal year 1964, the year this line of Liberals first took office. That deficit of $7.2 billion means that in addition to paying all of his other taxes, every taxpayer is being charged this year a further shortfall of approximately $500. Interest on that amount will cost each taxpayer about $50 a year, or $4 per month, until it has been repaid in two or three years. What a legacy to leave our children and their children! In our view, the government, if it had abided by its own guidelines which it set for everybody else with respect to pricing, could have cut a further $1.3 billion from its spending plans, which in turn would have meant a $100 tax break for the average Canadian taxpayer. Also, federal cash needs could have been lowered considerably. Such a tax break would have helped to lower wage demands and improve our real growth.
The administration's record with respect to inflation and unemployment, their second function, has been dismal. Under their supervision we have experienced, historically, high inflation and unemployment. How could it be otherwise when we review their irresponsible approach? I have mentioned that in the six years ended last October federal government spending jumped 151 per cent. During that same period, to help pay for that spending they increased the money system in Canada by 99 per cent. Real growth was 31.4 per cent. So is it a surprise that with the money supply being increased three times as fast as real growth we ended up with 55.3 per cent inflation in that period? Even the first six years of Liberal government in Ottawa were better. In the six years ended October, 1970, federal government spending went up 95 per cent. They created 43 per cent more money, experienced 34.7 per cent real growth, with inflation of 24 per cent.
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
But here is the crunch. When you compare the last two six-year periods with what we might call the Diefenbaker six-year period and the St. Laurent six-year period, we see in vivid colour the contrast between responsible government and irresponsible government. Let me put the figures on the record. In the six years ended October, 1964, mainly Diefenbaker years, federal government spending went up 33 per cent, money growth was less than 20 per cent and real growth was 32 per cent, compared with this administration's real growth of 31.4 per cent. But note, inflation in those six years was 7.7 per cent. Let me repeat that in those six years ended October, 1964, real growth was better than the real growth of our last six years, and inflation was 7.7 per cent in the six years, or less than one-seventh of the inflation experienced under this regime.
The St. Laurent years were comparable to the Diefenbaker years. In the six years ended October, 1958, real growth of almost 30 per cent, federal government spending increased by 35 per cent, money growth was 26 per cent, and inflation was 8.6 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They probably had better weather.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend says they probably had better weather. We know it was not. It was better government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not only are we faced with this high inflation record, but in the last six years of the Trudeau government we Find that the average unemployment has been higher than in any of the other three six-year periods. Faced with this record of irresponsibility, the administration tries to find other countries that have an even worse record than ours. In doing this they carefully ignore the fact that none of their comparisons are made with countries which have the rich resources we have. Have you ever seen them compare us with the records of other gas and oil exporting nations? Most of the countries plagued by inflation, such as Great Britain, import, manufacture and export virtually everything they deal in. They are not resource-rich as we are. In fact, we have made a good thing out of world inflation by selling our goods on the world market at inflated prices. Be that as it may, our record with respect to inflation is still worse than that of many countries. Take the United States, our main trading partner, for example. Last year our inflation was 9.3 per cent. In the United States, it was 5.1 per cent, and they did it without controls.
The government's own Figures disclose our relatively poor inflation record compared to that of the United States. If Switzerland, with no resources, has been able virtually to eliminate inflation, why must Canada, one of the richest countries in the world, have one of the world's worst inflation records? Not only do we have one of the world's worst records for inflation, but we have the worst record among the industrial nations for unemployment. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) says there is little he can do about the one million who will be out of work this year. One million people out of
4606

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
work is comparable to the entire working population of Montreal and its suburbs, or of the Toronto region, being idle-left, if you like, like ghost towns. Or again, one million people is equal to the work force of our four Atlantic provinces and the eastern part of Quebec being forced into idleness. Is that what the minister really means when he refers to stable recovery? We note the minister does not show tables in his budget document with respect to unemployment levels in other countries. Naturally, he would not. Even he could not stomach the evidence of this administration's ineptness in ensuring jobs for our people.
But if the government has failed in its first function of ensuring that governmental activities are run soundly and efficiently with the least possible taxation and with a minimum of deficit financing, and if it has failed in its second function of cultivating an economic climate that will provide full employment for those that wish to work, with a minimum of inflation, it is in its third function of structuring our activities to ensure that we remain competitive and able to hold our position as a trading nation that its deficiencies are most obvious. The government can, to some extent, befog the issue domestically, but not internationally.
Last year our current account trade deficit was S4.3 billion-that is higher than the $3.3 billion deficit of Great Britain, a nation we tended to pity-we even loaned them money as if we were well off. In the past two years this country's current account trade deficit was higher than that of any nation in the world. In fact, it was higher than the total deficit of the United States, Germany, Japan, France, Italy and the United Kingdom put together. And those six nations represent approximately 50 per cent of the world's wealth, while we have less than 3 per cent. If you find these figures startling, Mr. Speaker, look at page 8 of the minister's budget document. Faced with those figures, how can the minister tell us our economy is on the right track? The right track to where-oblivion?
The hard fact is that this country can pretend no longer that we are prosperous. Our prosperity has been conceived essentially on the basis of our taking in each other's washing. This is what the government has fostered with its orientation to government and service-oriented work for Canadians. A larger part of our economy is devoted to services than any western country or any country of the communist block or of the Third World. In 1967, 59 per cent of our labour force was engaged in the service industry, with 6 per cent in public administration alone. By 1976, service employment had risen to 65.5 per cent of our total, with 7.2 per cent employed in public administration. Producers of goods fell from 41 per cent of our work force in 1967, with 24 per cent in manufacturing, to 34.5 per cent by 1976 with 20.3 per cent in manufacturing.
This orientation to service activity resulted in Canada incurring a $10 billion deficit in end products world trade last year. It was $2 billion a few years ago. In short, we are becoming increasingly non-competitive in world markets. Our share of world trade is dropping. In the 1960s it was approximately 6 per cent of world exports. Today it is 4 per cent. In the last

three years our balance of payments deficit has averaged 2.7 per cent of our GNP. Some forecast it will be 7.5 per cent of GNP by the mid-1980s, due partly to a fall off in oil and gas exports which have shoved us up in recent years. The administration may play with figures with respect to our domestic activity, but it is in the external trade area that their incompetence is most apparent. You cannot fool the international market. That is why our dollar, which has fallen by as much as 40 per cent in relation to other currencies, has become known as the "Pierre peso". To all this the minister states there are no short-term solutions-no magic formulas for solving our economic woes. We agree. But where are the minister's long-term solutions? What does he see for the economy in 1980 or 1982? We do not know.
He will not even tell us about fiscal year 1979 which begins less than one year from now. That is why we in this party have asked for two-year projections for the next two years and three-year forecasts for the following three-year period. Let the nation see where we are going, assuming that the government's programs, whatever they are, work. After all, this government has spent the last five years getting us into this mess. Surely they can give us a glimpse of what they see for the next five years may get us out of the mess. If they will not produce such longer term figures, we can only assume that they themselves do not know where they are going or have no plans to relieve the situation other than day to day expediency. The truth, Mr. Speaker, is that it is political expediency, not economic responsibility, that has been the order of the day with this administration.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sheer nonsense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Americans, who expect to experience a real growth greater than our real growth this year, as they did last year, are willing to show five-year figures. Why cannot we? For example, in the United States they anticipate a real growth of 41/2 to 516 per cent per year for the next five years, which would be comparable to 516 to 6V2 per cent real growth in Canada. Does our government see that growth for Canada?
The United States figures show that by 1982 they will be down to a 4 per cent unemployment level. It would cut our unemployment level in half if we could reach that figure in Canada. But what is our plan so far as this administration is concerned? We in the Progressive Conservative party believe that the government should not only be acting on our immediate problems but should be putting into place what they feel is necessary to ensure that we do not have one million jobless or even more in coming years; that we do not have inflation of 4 to 6 per cent or even higher in coming years; that we do not have trade deficits which are the largest in the world which, in turn, require us to borrow foreign funds at high interest to keep us afloat.
This country is uniquely situated both geographically and in regard to resources. Those resources and our geographical location should make us one of the most prosperous nations in
April 4, 1977

the world. Rather than creating a hostile, often frustrating climate for business, we should make this an hospitable country for business activities. If we did that, those who are now routing business away from Canada would then route business into Canada, not only to serve our own markets but for international trade purposes as well.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are going bankrupt fast.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would not take much. First, it would be necessary for the government to satisfy the world of finance and business that they will be more responsible in their handling of our economy. Secondly, they must regulate business less. They must harass business less, and that means subjecting it to fewer administrative tribunals. Finally, they should give business a more assured tax position in the country. Business does not mind paying taxes. But they do mind having the rules changed abruptly which is little short of confiscation of their activities.
An end to the controls program at the earliest opportunity would help restore business and labour confidence. This government, however, does not seem to have the guts to take that type of action. Inflation is contained with responsible monetary and fiscal restraint, not controls. It takes guts to use those levers, however, and with this government political expediency comes first, economic responsibility and reality second. It is their indecision, their waffling that has undermined our prosperity. On the question of controls, even the Minister of Finance admits in his budget document:
The decline in profit margins in 1976 was primarily a reflection of slack markets in Canada and abroad, rather than the controls program. Most firms were unable to earn the margins which the guidelines permitted.
On the wage side, we know that Canadian wages have gone up under controls more than those in the United States where there are no controls. So why are the finance minister and the Prime Minister pussyfooting around telling us they are in a dilemma, not knowing what to do about controls? There should be no dilemma. Get rid of the damn things and start acting like men, instead of kids. This country needs men of courage running it, not a bunch of boy scouts who dither.
Some hon. members have asked what we would have done of an immediate nature if we had had the opportunity of bringing in a budget last Thursday. Let me summarize our position. My leader will, later in the debate, expand upon some of these points. Firstly, with regard to personal income tax, to help the economy resume an acceptable growth rate and to assist in the moderation of wage demands, we believe that a substantial personal tax cut should have been made, and would have been made if we had been in power, which would have given the greatest benefit to those earning less than $8,000 per year, with lesser benefits being realized by those earning between $8,000 and $16,000. The lower the income, the greater the benefit.
Secondly, with regard to manufacturers' sales tax, a reduction of this tax by us would have had a direct effect on price levels in this country. The tax itself is inflationary and is regressive in impact. It should have been reduced. It would
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
have been reduced if this had been our budget. Third, with regard to regional stimulation, although national in scope the greatest part of the burden of unemployment is borne by the five eastern provinces and by young persons entering the labour force. The principal thrust of our efforts to reduce unemployment would have been directed to these regions of the country and to this sector of the labour force.
To stimulate regions and sectors within the economy, some tax changes would have been made, including the following. Firstly, a tax rebate for small businessmen investing in research and development. The credit award could be as high as 75 per cent in the Atlantic region or Quebec, falling to, say, 25 per cent or less in provinces where the economy is performing better. Secondly, we would make tax credits available to corporations in compensation for high levels of tax paid because of the effects of inflation on inventory valuation and capital cost depreciation. In effect, a corporation would maintain two sets of books for tax purposes, one on the existing system, the other using a replacement value accounting system. A tax rebate up to the amount of difference in the tax liability between the two systems could be obtained by a corporation agreeing to invest the difference in a disadvantaged region. A lesser rebate would be allowed to those corporations investing in heavily industrialized areas. This would have been a more meaningful approach than the $300 million hand-out proposed by the administration with respect to inventory inflation. The government's proposal will have minimal effect in relieving unemployment where it is highest.
Referring to long-term tax contracts with companies investing in areas of regional disparity, we believe that the government should be willing to sign a tax contract. Under such a scheme a company which builds a plant in Newfoundland would sign an agreement exempting the operations of that plant from all tax until 150 per cent of the original investment had been recovered. A tax rebate for small businessmen faced with the burden of filling out forms for the federal bureaucracy would have been included in our budget if we had had an opportunity to bring one in last Thursday.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The government has no policy. They do nothing for the economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If I could touch on the small business investment incentive credit approach that we have advocated for some time, this investment credit would be available to any Canadian citizen who makes a direct investment in the equity of a Canadian-owned small business. The credit, which would be 50 per cent of qualified investments, to a maximum of $5,000 per year, would be either offset against the individual's income tax for the year or rebated directly to him. Qualifying investments would include new equity shares of corporations and direct participation in a proprietorship or partnership. A reduction in federal sales taxes on energy efficient cars would favour small cars and, hopefully, domestic production of those cars in addition to helping conserve energy and giving cheaper transportation for commuters.

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Further assistance to encourage the development of urban public transit system is required in Canada and should not have been overlooked by the budget last Thursday.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the dollar cost of all this?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne) asks, "What is the dollar cost of all this?" That hon. member should know. His Prime Minister promised $290 million to help urban transit in this country. We are saying that he should live up to that promise. We suggest it is better to spend $290 million, as suggested by the Prime Minister, on urban transportation needs in Canada rather than on such developments as Pickering.
Finally I come to the indexation of capital gains. They should not be assessed on the dollar appreciation of the capital asset but, rather, on a constant dollar appreciation; that is, the appreciation over and above the inflation that has taken place over the period of acquisition to sale. The measure of inflation could be the same as the Department of National Revenue uses to index personal income tax brackets. I emphasize that these tax reductions would not increase the federal deficit, as they would be more than offset by the $1.3 billion that I indicated earlier could be shaved from this administration's spending estimates.
Other policies we would have introduced to ensure a smooth transition to a decontrolled economy, if we had had the opportunity last Thursday, would have been more long-term forecasting of federal revenues and expenditures, as well as forecasts of expected economic growth, inflation and job creation. Each budget should issue forecasts for the two fiscal years ahead. For example, in the case of the March 31, 1977, budget there should have been federal projections for the fiscal years 1978 and 1979. In addition, performance targets for government and the economy should be issued for the three further fiscal years following those projections; in this case, to fiscal year 1982. Longer range forecasts and targets would enable business, labour and other levels of government to plan strategies for the future.
A national economic conference with multipartite representation to discuss the future course of the economy would have been suggested and advocated in our budget. Items on the agenda would have been the methods by which all levels of government could reduce their share of the gross national product. What is the realistic growth target for the nation, year by year? How do we achieve that target, with a minimum of inflation? What is full employment? How do we restructure our economy to be more effective in world trade? I have already referred to that. Zero-based budgeting in certain federal departments at least should be introduced on a trial basis. This would mean all items in the budget are reviewable, ending the present argument that most spending items are statutory or at least untouchable when budgets are being settled.
While to this point I have dealt mainly with colourless statistics, the really tragic result of this government's incompetence in handling our economy is that hundreds of thousands of Canadians are being demoralized. Their outlooks and their ambitions are being dashed. Canada, the land of opportunity, is becoming to them the land of discouragement and disenchantment. Be they university graduates, young farmers or factory workers, they feel the country holds out little promise. It has become a country in which the Prime Minister tells them that if they do not like their job opportunities, then go to another country. He said that his heart does not bleed for them.
True, you cannot get blood from a stone. But it is time our government showed compassion for those who are feeling the brunt of the economic morass into which this administration has led us. On the other hand we have those who, while they may not be unemployed, are watching their savings erode. Their hopes are disappearing with respect to owning a home. They see this happening as a result of inflation. As we think of those who are out of work and finding it hard to get by, it is interesting to note how easily the government keeps defining and redefining the problems and how easily it holds rich men's conferences such as the one in Toronto to discuss the problems still further. They point out the obvious. They point out that many people are moving to our cities from the country; that they are discouraged; that their sense of purpose and their sense of individuality is being shaken. Hope is lost, they point out, among many Canadian people today. The administration, however, is void of fresh ideas for harnessing the energies of these vital people. Instead, the Liberals suggest that we should be reconciled to less growth, which means more unemployment. Like typical technocrats, they suggest it is the goals of yesterday that are wrong, not that they are wrong in failing to allow us to achieve those goals. In the flood of human initiative they say, "Lower the water." We say, "Raise the bridge."
This human tragedy is perhaps better portrayed in a verse written by a former employee of the Globe and Mail, the late Dan O'Connell. He wrote of his experience, having shifted to the city, as follows:
The rolling farmland by the lake,
The mirthful matins in the brake.
The cozy cottage ivy-clad,
The homestead hallowed as a lad,
The stream that teemed with speckled trout,
The homemade rod that fished them out,
The dream of home, a loving wife,
And each ambition lost throught life,
Like ghosts they haunt your heart,
While dead you tread the city's mart.
That is the lot, unfortunately, of thousands of Canadians today. In view of this and in view of the motion that we have before us, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), that all the words after "that" in the motion before us be deleted and the following substituted therefor:

April 4, 1977

This House does not have confidence in the government's budgetary policy by reason of its failure to provide the active economic leadership and foresight needed to reduce unemployment and inflation and encourage confidence and growth in the Canadian economy.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser)-Reason for failure of Rail West to receive orders for hoppers cars; the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith)-Penitentiaries- Proposed new institution for Manitoba-Possibility of site at Churchill or Lynn Lake; the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald)-Provision of boxcars for shipment of potatoes- Government action.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the government, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stevens.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, recently the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and myself were on a television program. We were asked a question with regard to predicting the budget. The only prediction 1 would make at that time was that the hon. member for York-Simcoe would find it more difficult to criticize than I would. That has turned out to be correct. I must congratulate the hon. member for York-Simcoe for having been able to criticize what was essentially a budget that out-Toried the Tories as far as newspaper reports are concerned.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1 wish to refer for a few moments to the statements made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. He said that this country needs to become a more hospitable country for business. I do not know how much more hospitable this budget could be for business. Out of the tax cuts given of
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
$1.5 billion, less than $400 million went in the form of tax cuts to individuals. More than $1.1 billion went to business. Perhaps the hon. member for York-Simcoe is suggesting that the less than $400 million that went to individuals should have been turned over to business as well. I do not know how much more hospitable we can be in this country to business.
The crux of our problem at the moment and the reason that we find ourselves in this incredible situation is that this government, in response to pressure from the Conservative party, has out-Toried the Tories and has placed its reliance completely on business instead of using its own common sense.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about pressure from the NDP?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When there was pressure from the NDP and the government responded to it, we did not have the unemployment levels we have at this time. There is something to be said for those minority government days. Perhaps it would have been just as well had the government listened to the NDP again, because they certainly do better for the country than when they listen to the Conservatives. In describing this budget, my leader said that in economic terms it is stupid and in human terms it is cruel. I think he was being excessively kind. It is certainly that. In some ways this budget is beyond contempt.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: "Beneath" contempt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To beat this budget is almost unnecessary in light of the universal condemnation that has been heaped upon it from every quarter of our society, with the exception of a few business people. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider the following. The government is giving concessions to business in order to try to save itself. It has totally run out of ideas. It is so lacking in ideas that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) took pleasure in announcing that he was running around consulting businessmen as to what possibly might be in the budget. 1 am not suggesting the minister told businessmen what would be in the budget, but he certainly made a point of saying he was seeking their advice. If he did get their advice, it is certainly bad advice.
We have had a history, over the past five years at least, of tax concessions to business. There has been an almost direct relationship between the amount of tax concessions we have given to business and the decay of the economy. Tax concessions simply do not work. I would not object to concessions to business if there were some evidence to support the notion that the way to get people back to work is to make these concessions. The C. D. Howe Institute, in a recent report, clearly made the case after extensive research-and I am not quoting from an NDP document, as my friends on the right will recognize-that there is no evidence to support the idea that tax concessions to business have had a stimulating effect on the economy or have created extra employment.
A former Minister of Finance sent out a questionnaire asking business whether all the great give-away programs such as depreciation allowances and a lower rate of taxation stimulated employment. He received virtually a negative reply. This

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
is not a question of saying we do not want to give it to business. If I believed, and the evidence was there, that the way to get people back to work was to make it somewhat easier for business by reducing the taxation on business, I might not like it in terms of equity but I would go along with in terms of getting this country going. However, we have destroyed equity by what we have done in relation to what we are giving to the ordinary taxpayers and giving to business. We have got less than nothing from it.
I say this country has not been inhospitable to business. I quote as follows from a recent speech by the Hon. Eric Kierans at McGill University on September 23, 1976:
For the life of me, 1 cannot understand the hostility of the business community to the Trudeau government. It cannot be on the basis of what the federal government has done for, literally, big business has never had it so good. With the exception of the United Kingdom, I doubt that any nation in the world has given its corporate 1,000 a more handsome gift package of subsidies, tax allowances, two-year write-offs, deductibility of merger costs, cheap loans, export credits and insurance than our present Trudeau government...
The goal of the corporation is profit, or at least 99'/2 per cent profit since a half-cent of every profit dollar is given away for charitable purposes.
You can see that Mr. Kierans was trying to be fair in his argument. Then he said:
One cannot say that the corporate sector has not achieved its purpose during the last five years . . . Profits increased from $7.7 billion in 1970 to $17.8 billion in 1975, or an increase of 131 per cent, and yet "unfriendly Ottawa"-
I point this out to my avenging angel, the hon. member for York-Simcoe who puts himself forward as being the defender of the underdog-
-in the words of one outstanding Canadian chief executive, "does not understand free enterprise". And despite popular impression, corporate income tax rates declined during that five-year period. In 1970 corporations paid an effective federal rate of 29.6 per cent on their $7.7 billion in profits. In 1975, the effective federal rate was 26.6 per cent on profits of $17.8 billion. But who, listening to businessmen, would have believed this?
Let me be quite frank and ask you this. Just what will satisfy the unhappy 1,000? What will bring to an end the whining, whimpering and outright misrepresentation of the successes of the past five years?
Certainly not the comments and interventions of hon. friends on my right as expressed by the hon. member for York-Simcoe. This is a myth that is being perpetrated and compounded in this House. The hon. member said the root of our problem is the hostility of the Canadian government to business. I wish they were as hostile to the poor of this country as they are to business. The poor would be better off.
Past concessions to business to some extent account for the mess we are in right now. We have to say: Had we not made all these tax concessions, particularly in the area of depreciation allowances, and encouraged industry to over invest because there was a tax benefit involved in that, we would not be faced with the situation where industry has so much capacity that it cannot use. In fact, less than 80 per cent of that capacity is in use. That is one of the reasons for the high level of unemployment. How, then, does the government justify saying in the budget that we can stimulate more capital investment by increasing the profits of business, when they cannot even use the investment they have now? Probably the investment they have now is what is contributing to the high level of unemployment.

This morning it was my pleasure to pick up a book by Tony Westall, a very distinguished Canadian journalist.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hardly a raving socialist.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is called "The New Society". I guess he took his theme from some of the words the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke last year. Westall talks about corporation profits and what happens in a cyclical period. He writes:
Corporation profits, which had fallen sharply in 1970, rebounded to rise 12.8 per cent in 1972, 35 per cent in 1973, 27 per cent in 1974, before turning down 3 per cent in 1975. Part of the surge in profits was cyclical as the government spurred expansion, and part of it was simply the result of inflation: as world prices soared, inventories of materials held by corporations increased in value and returned superprofits when they were sold. But when the corporation restocked at the new higher prices, much of the windfall profit was absorbed in working capital. Nevertheless, the corporations had made a real gain, although it was in the nature of a one-time capital gain rather than a normal operating profit.
The point I want to make is that one of the measures which my friend, the hon. member for York-Simcoe, did not criticize was the move of the government in this budget toward inflation accounting, which is to take into account the fact that as corporations and companies sell off their stock, their inventory, they have to replace their inventory at a somewhat higher cost and therefore some of the profit is lost in the process. I would be more inclined to go along with inflation accounting, a measure that the government has brought into this budget, if during the period of high profits the government had put an extra surtax on the profits that came from inventory realization. That was not done, nor was there any outcry that there be any kind of indexing on inventory profit, that in fact they should be paying more because this was found money, it was an inventory profit, they bought cheap and were selling dear. Nothing was said among the business community about that. But the minute it starts to work the other way, the government has to bail them out.
There is no balancing. The government does not say, "Sure, you are going to suffer some losses", or, "You will need more capital," or, "You will need a larger cash flow in order to replace your inventories. But you did have profits in the past and you did benefit from inflation because of the increase in your inventory value, and surely one should offset the other." But no, the government says solicitously, "We will give you inflation accounting as well, and give you a few hundred million dollars to compensate you for this business risk". This is the kind of thing that my friend, the hon. member for York-Simcoe, says is inhospitable. He says it does not create a hospitable climate for business in this country.
I would have been far more impressed if during the period when those inventories were rising and being sold off, the hon. member for York-Simcoe had said that the consumers who were buying them should have been able to buy them at cost plus a mark-up for which those inventories had been acquired. But I suppose that is not the correct business attitude to have. What is the point of being in business if you do not speculate? But you speculate only one way with the consumers.
April 4, 1977

This budget does a number of other things which I think are most unsatisfactory. We went through a period called the Carter period. The Conservative government commissioned a study on the taxation system. When it was completed and presented to parliament, it stated that Canada had one of the worst tax systems in the world; it had many loopholes that simply had to be closed. The government, very hesitantly, far short of what Carter recommended, started to close some of those loopholes. Now the government realizes that it made a terrible mistake because in closing those loopholes it has aroused the ire of the hon. member for York-Simcoe who is saying the government is inhospitable to business. Therefore, the government is now proceeding to open the loopholes again in the budget.
The argument is that it is not worth closing them because not much revenue is derived from closing them. Not only that, but we have to provide some incentives in the way of stock options, reduced taxation on capital gains, this despite the fact that capital gains are still only taxed at half the regular rate. I cannot understand the solicitude of the government with respect to capital gains. I could perhaps support the argument that is being made that the value of the capital should be indexed if we had full taxation. But where is the rationale and the justice which says that a guy who works in a shop, a guy who works at the lathe, or a guy who teaches school or performs some other function for which he gets wages or a salary pays on the total amount of what he earns, but the person who gets his income from speculating on the stock market and who makes a capital gain is twice as worthy and therefore has to pay only half the tax? That is a very inhospitable climate for business, 1 must say, particularly when this budget says that one-third dividend on the tax credit is not enough, the government will make it one-half. The budget states that the government has given up the idea of taking stock options as a form of increasing a person's benefit in a company. Now they will let people take stock options and take the benefit without having to bear taxation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This really helps the little guy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I love these little guys at the top, and I am delighted that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) feels so strongly about the little guy that he designates him as the president, vice-president or the chairman of the board. I think it is delightful to see his solicitude for the little guy at that level, and I commend him for it.
Let me return to something more serious than the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. Let me say what is galling about this measure. It is quite true that perhaps there is no great revenue loss in this matter, but this is a matter of principle which I think is important. You are going to say to the guy in the shop whose wages are now controlled by AIB, "Don't complain about being controlled by AIB, because it is for the national good". It is for the national good for him to be controlled, but it is not for the national good for his employer to be controlled.
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
Even when the AIB says they will try to control executive wages, the government realizes it has made a terrible mistake in even trying to move in the direction of equity. Equity does not work for this government; it creates too many problems. So they say, "All right. What AIB cannot do through the front door we will do through the budget by the back door". In other words, "Executive salaries will not be increased officially as it is not permitted under AIB regulations, because that would make the troops in the factories very restless. Therefore, let us give it to the executive in the form of stock options so we can increase their real income, the amount of money they earn, without having to incur tax liability, and then we can say we did not do it through the AIB".
I think a modern society can no longer live without an incomes policy. This party has always supported an incomes policy. In principle, a democratic socialist party has to support an incomes policy, and the chief reason we object to the anti-inflation program is that it is not an incomes policy. It is grossly unfair. It is a distortion and a dishonour to anything one might call an incomes policy, because it sits on one group of people and tells those people that they have to bear the brunt of restraint, and other people are let off in one way or another. If the government finds it really has some control on some things besides wages and salaries, it devises a convenient budget in which they can slip through and evade those controls.
Like all ministers of finance before him, the Minister of Finance keeps talking about U.S. recovery. He keeps waiting for a U.S. recovery to save us. The Yanks are always coming over the hill with their cavalry to save us. But I do not think that will happen this time. Like all countries in the world, the United States has its own problems. In fact, because of its problems it is becoming more protectionist. That is not a criticism of the United States. They have their problems, and the Americans have elected a government to try to deal with them.
I do not want to quarrel with the kinds of measures the United States government takes, but what becomes obvious is that by having the degree of foreign investment we have in Canada-mostly United States foreign investment-whatever benefits it may have in periods of boom, we now see the disadvantages at a time like this. If we have to expand production, and if we have to provide jobs, we have to do it in our own country; it should not be done by another country through its branch plants. However, that is what is happening, and even though the American economy may recover, there is no guarantee that our economy will follow suit until long after that recovery is full-blown. We have to find our own solutions, instead of hoping and praying for somebody else's recovery. We should hope for an American recovery because we are good neighbours and we would like to see the Americans do well, but to go on the assumption that somebody else is going to save our skins is a mistake. It is to some extent an insult to the parliament of Canada and to the people of Canada to think

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
that our government is so impotent that it cannot devise its own solutions to these problems.
When we look at some of the things the government has done, we are shocked at the opposite directions in which those things go. On the one hand the government wants to increase consumption. It feels that consumption is necessary. Every economist who looks at our economy says the consumption pattern is weak and that we have to find some way of stimulating consumption in order to get people back to work. What did the government do in its unlamented, late budget? The government introduced improvements in registered retirement savings plans and in other plans of that kind in order to encourage saving. With one hand the government is trying to encourage consumption, and with the other hand it is trying to encourage saving. What does the government really want? How does the government really see society? This must be one of the most confused governments in the history of this country, and that takes some doing because we have had many confused governments over the years.
In a way, I feel sorry for the Minister of Finance. He is a big, strapping fellow and one should not feel sorry for him. But I do not envy his job. I hear rumours and read in the press- which is the same thing as hearing rumours-that the minister is considering leaving his post or even leaving politics. 1 can understand how he feels. Trying to do something with the job he has been handed is not an enviable task. I think the difficulty which exists is the idea-which almost everyone on the government side and, unfortunately, almost everyone in the official opposition has-that the way to save the country is to save big business and to give it many tax concessions.
That is like the American, Charlie Wilson, theory which is, "What is good for General Motors is good for the country". I do not want to talk disparagingly about businessmen. I know many businessmen, and they are quite intelligent. They know their jobs, but they certainly do not know how to run the country. It is not their responsibility to run the country, and they really do not see beyond their own particular problems. A government which is so business-oriented that it keeps looking in that particular corner to find an answer is very much at the root of our problem.
The reason I say this is that one of the things that impressed me-this is to show that sometimes my better instincts get the best of my partisanship, and I have to be very careful about that-was the broadcast made by the Prime Minister a year ago Christmas. In that broadcast he talked about a new society. He started to lay out some ideas to the effect that the market system was not working the way it was supposed to work, which we in this party have been saying for a long time. I suppose that was unfortunate, because the Prime Minister was immediately labelled as a socialist for saying just a few sentences. He did not get very far, but there was a lot of truth to what he was saying at that time. We are becoming a different kind of society, and what is aggravating and devastating this country is that neither the Liberal party nor the Conservative party want to recognize that unemployment is not something which will just blow away. It is not something

which can be corrected by a little more or a little less deficit financing or by a little more or a little fewer concessions to business. Fundamental changes are taking place in our society, and neither the government nor the Official Opposition are taking them into consideration. This is the central problem. Our pattern of consumption has changed. The demography of our country has changed.
In trying to prepare for this debate my mind kept going back to what I remember of the depression and to what I remember reading. Recently 1 read an interesting book which brought the depression more vividly to my recollection. The book was called "The Dirty Thirties". That book reminded me of what is going on now in this chamber. It is R. B. Bennett and Hoover all over again. They said that prosperity was just around the corner. Perhaps with the best of intentions those blind men could not see that their society was going through a special kind of crisis. The unemployment they were looking at was not something that was going to go away. We are still talking about balanced budgets, the gold standard and blasting our way into the markets of Europe. Those men could not see that the blight of virtually a whole generation at that time was something different, that something fundamental had been altered in the market system and that business was not able to do the job. At first Keynes was not listened to. 1 was not until the war was over that anybody paid attention to John Maynard Keynes. It took a war to get us out of that mess.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We need another war.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For ten solid years there was a mess because the government did not realize that business was not going to pull us out of our troubles and that prosperity was not around the corner. To some extent I think we are going through the same thing. Granted, unemployment is not the hardship it was in the thirties. No one will argue that it is, thanks to many of the ideas my party has been able to impress upon governments over the years.
There has been some amelioration of hardship. We have had unemployment insurance and various other kinds of security measures which take some of the sting out of our problems. They create other problems in the process, but unemployment is still less of a personal tragedy. However, it becomes more and more a personal tragedy as the years go by and as a whole generation finds itself without the opportunity to work. Fundamentally, society cannot exist if people get out of the habit of working. Even if they can survive, our society cannot exist if we break it into two classes, one class having jobs or having the opportunity to have jobs, and the other class being made up of those who are unemployed and who have to be supported by those who work.
We have only to look around this country and others to see what happens during long periods of chronic unemployment. We can see what it does to people's attitudes and how difficult these are to correct later when there are enough jobs. When we talk about the present situation, we have to put it into
April 4, 1977

perspective and realize things will not always be this way. We are told that the baby boom will be over in ten years and then, instead of high levels of unemployment, we will have labour shortages. We will need all sorts of social structures to deal with this, and we will not have the manpower for it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are hoping for a war.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Surely there has to be an alternative. Surely we do not have to butcher every generation to get us out of the mess of unemployment. Professor Morgan of the University of Toronto published a little book called "Permanent War" in which he asked if it is not possible for us to summon up ideas, sinews and attitudes to find in peacetime and do in peacetime those things we do in war.
Let us examine where the resources will come from. We are using resources like mad at the moment and not getting anything back except something that is destroying the fibre of the young people and the not so young. These young people have been trained to work and want to work, and parents are trying to impart the work ethic to them. But where are the jobs? How long can this situation go on until they stop searching for work or stop caring and, instead, start asking, "Who needs to work, anyway? There are not enough jobs and no work that can be done".
As a social democratic party we believe in the dignity of work. We think society has a responsibility to ensure that those who want to work have jobs, particularly when there are jobs to be done whether it be for our own poor, work for the future, or work for other countries. We almost need an internal Marshall aid program for the same reasons that the United States brought it in after World War II-as much to save Europe as to save the United States. It is for that reason we must do something more than mouth the kind of platitudes about the road to salvation being the road through business incentives, but this is what we have been hearing from the government and from the Official Opposition.
Mr. Speaker, let me make a few suggestions. One thing we should do immediately is start lowering the age of eligibility for old age pensions. The time has come to do that from a moral point of view, from a humane point of view and from economic necessity. Many older people have told me they would like to stop working, perhaps not at age 60 but, say, 63 or 64. Many young people want to work but have not got the jobs, and the older ones want to know why they should keep on working, thus depriving the young of the opportunity. Young people tell us to retire their parents because they want to work themselves and the parents would like to take it easy. Lowering the age could be done on a gradual basis, one year at a time.
We should also be working with provincial governments on arrangements to ban overtime except in exceptional circumstances. What justification is there for some people working overtime while others are looking for work? Is it because it is convenient for business to do it that way? What sort of society is it that cannot organize itself better than that? We have to redistribute income not only for moral purposes but for eco-
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
nomic necessity. We have reached a point where our middle and upper middle classes save their money and do not spend it on consumer goods. We have reached the point of satiation for many people. We cannot use the old ploy of tax relief. That is all right if you give it to the 20 per cent of the people at the bottom of the scale who will spend the money. It is not a question of morality any more; it is now an economic imperative to redistribute income in order to provide jobs in society.
There are many things we should be doing in the area of public works. How are we going to build an urban transit system ten years hence if we have labour shortages? Railroad beds have to be rebuilt and many other things have to be done which will mean jobs and people going back to work and something useful for society coming out of it.
We need more public housing, and we need to do something about the environment. The columnist Richard Gwynn made some suggestions, as could any of us. We are spending $4 billion for unemployment insurance, and $1.2 billion of this budget is going to business. If you add all the makeshift programs of the government, you are talking about $6 billion or $8 billion. Imagine what that kind of money could do to stimulate the economy and provide the social infrastructure for a civilized life for ourselves and those who come after us. There is so much to be done-museums, preservation of historic buildings-anything is better than putting people on the pogey. We have a budget that is not only going to leave them there but is going to put more people on it. We have run out of ideas and do not know how to handle the situation.
