subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am delighted to rise today not only on behalf of my Villeneuve constituents, but also of all low and middle income Canadians. I intend to deal with the budget speech which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) made on Thursday, March 31.
Mr. Speaker, this is in fact my first term in office in the House of Commons, for it is in 1974 that the people in the Villeneuve constituency elected me to represent them here. I have therefore been exposed to a somewhat limited number of budget speeches made by the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). Yet, although I may remain a member of the House for a long time to come, I am sure that I shall never
4614

funny but when you witness the performance of the Minister of Finance you realize that the third sentence is certainly not the easiest to believe.
When we consider a budget such as the one under study, a budget which has nothing to offer the Canadian taxpayer, we tend to believe that the government is not proposing any new measure to solve these problems, especially current problems such as unemployment. There is however one favourable result-this budget will not create a deficit. But, Mr. Speaker, that is the last straw. This year, not only do people with small incomes have nothing positive to expect from the budget but there will be a tremendous deficit to boot.
As I said earlier, a family man with four children earning $7,000 a year will have the joy of saving $4 in income tax next year. You know, Mr. Speaker, the kind of deficit that such a person will have to bear with his children. Believe it or not, he will have to bear a deficit of more than $7 billion. Mr. Speaker, that is what I call paying dearly for nothing. 1 for one would be ashamed of meeting my fellow Canadians if I had to present a budget such as the one introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). But it is true that the finance minister meets his fellow citizens on Bay Street or St. James Street where he knows he will find friends after having introduced his budget.
As I said earlier, the budget brings no comfort, no hope for the low income taxpayer. Not only did the minister neglect or forget this fact, he added insult to injury. In fact, when speaking to reporters he said that Canadians were not ready for self imposed wage controls and that anti-inflation controls would have to be kept on for an unspecified period.
1 believe, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians are at least as able to control themselves as the government is proud to present an annual deficit of more than $7 billion. It should not be up to ordinary citizens to enforce anti-inflation controls but rather to the finance minister who seems to have difficulty controlling his own expenditures.
Like in his last budget, the minister insists that the government tries to prevent any drastic change to the tax and monetary policy. Last year, he was saying about the same thing: we must not rock the boat. The government did not rock the boat but the economy remained in the same condition, whatever grinning Jean-Luc Pepin may say. Instead of giving us statistics indicating that inflation is not as severe as before, I should like to see the same Mr. Pepin shopping the same way lower income Canadians do. Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, Social Crediters do not agree with the budget of the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One Social Crediter!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All of them!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are all by yourself!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They will come back. If you check the ratio between Liberals and Social Crediters, 1 think there are more Social Crediters than Liberals. It is obvious that the monetary
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
and fiscal system is showing a deficit. So this is no time to hesitate and run around in circles.
Action is needed, and the sooner the better, to change the deficiencies in the system and ensure that our enormous natural resources can be developed. We have the means, the equipment, the expertise and the workers needed. How come the economy cannot undertake all those projects that would benefit Canada as a whole? Because the current monetary system is not in tune with the facts of life in our modern world. This is why the Social Credit Party of Canada has been urging a basic reform of this obsolete system of ours. This is why we cannot accept the kind of fiddling we are getting from the Minister of Finance, who will not take the aggressive initiatives that are so vital. He is now saying: "Let us wait, let us not move too much, the problem may disappear by itself'. 1 submit that problem will not disappear by itself. If we want it to disappear, we will have to take adequate steps.
We will have to reform the economic and financial system. Of course that reform is not welcome by those with a vested interest, those who partake in the Minister of Finances' generosity. Clearly, financiers taking advantage of a scarce money situation to sink individuals, governments and small businesses into debt want no change at all. They prefer that the government do not rock the boat, they prefer getting tax exemptions on their investments into businesses that must borrow to remain in business.
This is what we are fighting, Mr. Speaker. Abraham Lincoln once said: "You can fool some of the people some of the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time". This is still true in our days. Canadians will not be made by the Minister of Finance to believe that this budget serves the needs and aspirations of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to turn for a few minutes to one specific aspect of Thursday's budget speech, one aspect involving more than 400,000 Canadians. I am referring of course to all those who trusted the government and entered into the home ownership savings program. When the government launched the program three years ago, they said that all those who did not own a house were eligible. They also stated that the money thus set aside could be used either for the purchase of a house or for the purchase of furniture for the spouse's house. These were, Mr. Speaker, precise rules and all those who registered for the programs were prepared to comply with them.
Today, the minister changes the rules of the game. He tells us that if the spouse already owns a house, we cannot be eligible under the home ownership plan. He also says that we will not be allowed to spend the money on furniture any more. Mr. Speaker, according to me, when you play cards and one of the players tries to change the rules in the middle of the game he is called a cheater because he does not comply with the rules which were set up at the beginning. Today, the Minister of Finance says there has been so-called abuses in these programs and he wants to change the rules of the game when more than 400,000 Canadians have accepted to play according to the rules as set originally.
80012 - 1414

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Cullen
People who started to participate in the home ownership savings plan before the minister's statement in his budget speech should in my opinion under their vested interests be able to continue to participate in those plans for which they applied in good faith when the minister set up this program three years ago.
I have no objection to the minister changing the rules of the game for those who will be going into those programs in the future. They will be doing so knowing that they are subject to new rules. But I think that to eliminate the vested interests of those who participated in that program before the minister's statement would be as unfair and ignominious as could possibly be. I think that is called cheating, whether it is in a card game or in the implementation of regulations by a minister. So 1 ask the minister to reconsider his decision about those who were already participating in his home ownership insurance program before his budget speech.
I think his legal background, which allowed him to learn how despicable and contrary to legal principles retroactive legislation can be, should lead him to refuse to change the rules of the game after people have already entered the game.
Mr. Speaker, I heard several remarks since I rose to speak but I would be remiss if I did not congratulate the Minister of Finance for the only thing that deserves congratulating in his speech. 1 am talking about the courage he had to get up and read a budget speech in the House of Commons, a budget so disastrous that I would certainly not have dared to make it if I had been in his boots.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That will never happen!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope the House can bring this government to reason and have it take concrete steps to put the economy back on its feet. It is time to stop being afraid to rock the boat.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these are tough times to be Minister of Finance or, for that matter, Minister of Manpower and Immigration, but I congratulate my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), for having the audacity and the courage to add to the deficit, recognizing that the economy in fact needed some form of stimulus to help it along. At the same time he showed the sense of responsibility necessary not to do as opposition parties seem to be advocating, that is, to blow the lid off this "pressure cooker" of deficit financing. I think that what we have here is a Minister of Finance who has accepted his responsibility but has taken the risk of increasing the deficit which we now have, at the same time recognizing that he could not give in as the members of the opposition would have him do.
I think the reaction of the opposition parties could have been anticipated in advance, with the NDP critic suggesting that we in fact had been too generous to business, that we had in fact out-toried the Tories, and then the Tories suggesting that we had not been generous enough. What we also find is the rather

interesting phenomenon of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) now out-NDPing the NDP. He suggested substantial tax cuts for those on low and fixed incomes, and said that they should be substantial. I noted that with all the statistics he quoted in his speech, not one mention did he make of how substantial he thought it should be, or by how much more should the deficit be increased.
You cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. You cannot criticize the government for having too large a deficit and then, on the other hand, say that we should have made more substantial tax cuts to assist persons on low and fixed incomes, that we should have cut out manufacturers' sales tax and done a myriad other things.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Read my speech.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I understand the hon. member for York-Simcoe's leader is going to flesh out some of these suggestions which have been made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, so we will be listening very carefully.
Hon. members may recall that when I introduced our employment strategy in the House last October, I pointed out that no priority is more important to the government than helping Canadians to find work. That commitment was valid then, and it is valid now. It has been reinforced by the announcement made by the Minister of Finance about our plans to increase funding for the employment strategy.
As I have previously pointed out, the Canadian economy, despite recent high unemployment, has been showing considerable growth in the number of private sector jobs available. In the past two years employment grew by about 200,000 each year, a greater growth than occurred in the middle or late 1960's when unemployment rates were below 5 per cent.
Our basic challenge continues to be the influx of young people and women into the labour market. Our labour force grows faster than the number of job opportunities the economy is generating. That is the fundamental reason why unemployment has grown and why we have abnormally high unemployment rates this winter.
In outlining the five-year employment strategy last fall, I pointed out that one of the key features would be flexibility. We plan to expand or contract our employment strategy investments as necessary, to add or subtract program elements, and to ensure that the general shape of the strategy is continuously appropriate to the labour market and economic circumstances which prevail from time to time. Accordingly, we have maintained a close watch on the economic circumstances and on the performance of the programs in the employment strategy. This close watch and continuing review have twice enabled us to determine that increases, particularly in the direct job creation component of the strategy, were both desirable and warranted. In other words, we monitored and we were able to prove our case.
April 4, 1977

The first occasion was last December when I announced a doubling of the Local Initiatives Program to the level of $200 million. We are now benefiting from the consequent increase in jobs and will continue to do so through June, when the program ends.
Last Thursday the Minister of Finance announced, as part of the government's general approach to the management and recovery of the economy, a further increase of $100 million in our commitment to the employment strategy bringing the funding for this year along to a total of $458 million.
Taken in conjunction with our other important investments in employment programs, we will be spending some $1.2 billion on programs either to train people for jobs, or help them find jobs, or to make jobs for them. There are very few countries in the world which do as much in either absolute or proportional terms.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are, 1 realize, some who would have us do vastly more-launch some sort of job creation program or perform some miracle of fiscal policy that would, theoretically, guarantee a job for everyone who might want to work. There are those who will say that what we are doing, despite its scale, is far too little. It would indeed be wonderful if we could abolish unemployment with one blow. I want to assure members that if that were possible, we would not hesitate to do so.
The alternatives have been carefully canvassed, reviewed, and considered. There is simply no easy means of achieving all of the objectives at once.
A gigantic program of job creation, running into the billions of dollars, is not a practical proposition, because there are limits to the feasible scope of any one approach to the reduction of unemployment. But it is not practical, as well, simply because there are limits on the degree to which governments can increase their spending without both inflationary and broad social consequences.
Even those European countries which have been most deeply committed to the motion of full employment have found that they cannot guarantee it. Some of them have attempted to reduce their own unemployment by sending foreign workers back home-a policy of exporting their unemployment. Other countries have launched crash programs only to find that much of what they were doing has no effect. They are simply paying to create jobs that would have been created in any event. Still others have adopted policies which seem to have some limited success in maintaining employment, but at the cost of productivity and international competitiveness.
Our employment strategy has been formulated with these realities in mind. I believe that we can take pride in its good sense and its success. We have developed a realistic employment strategy which contains elements directed toward fundamental long run problems as well as the immediate needs for job creation. It is accompanied by an immigration policy which brings to Canada people who are needed to work rather
The Budget-Mr. Cullen
than an excess of people to swell the ranks of the unemployed, or be sent home when not wanted. The employment related programs within the strategy have very little substitution effect. The money goes to creating new jobs, not to paying for things that would have been done in any event. They are probably more precisely aimed at real problems than those of any other country.
I would like to be able to say that our employment strategy will itself bring the country to full employment levels, but that is beyond the capacity of any set of programs or the immediate power of any government. For one thing, we simply do not have the funds. Our employment strategy will altogether create over 600,000 man-months of employment. To reduce unemployment to some target level of 5 per cent or 4 per cent, even through these highly efficient programs, would cost literally billions. Nobody, I am sure, would suggest that these billions should be found by cutting out other federal programs which are so important to our economic and social well-being; nor could we add the vast sums which would be required to existing government expenditures. We must, and I believe can, learn to use our resources even more wisely and more productively.
Our dilemma is that we face real limitations on what can be expended for training and for job creation, at the same time as we must pay far larger sums to sustain those who lack either jobs or training. We are, through the new unemployment insurance legislation, moving to permit people to use these income maintenance payments in the most productive way possible to take needed additional training or participate in job creation projects. The financial linkage of our new unemployment insurance, training, and job creation systems offers great potential scope for the future. It is a way of providing people who are unemployed with training and with jobs, rather than cheques. If we are successful, we will be able to reduce unemployment more without increasing the level of our expenditures.
Our priority at the moment, however, must clearly be to add to the number of jobs available. Virtually all of the increase in our employment strategy funding will go to programs that create new employment, often with an experience or training component, in either community or private sector work.
We are accordingly adding immediately about $50 million to the Canada Works program, to bring it to a full quarter of a billion dollars. This increase to the Canada Works program has been made possible by the enthusiastic reception which the first round received. Over 8,200 applications have been submitted, to a total value of some $435 million. The increase will permit the ministerial advisory boards to recommend the funding of approximately 3,150 projects on this first round with the assurance that there is still no general shortage of good projects from which to choose.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the supper hour I indicated that we will be adding immediately about $50 million to the Canada Works program. That will bring it up to a full quarter of a billion dollars. I indicated we had received about 8,200 applications for a total value of $435 million. The increase will permit ministerial advisory boards to recommend the funding of approximately 3,150 projects on this first round, with the assurance that there is still no general shortage of good projects from which to choose.
The high quality of the projects is a critical element in the success of a sound job creation program. I have been most pleased with the extremely careful and responsible job that the the ministerial advisory boards have been doing in assigning priorities to projects. I have also been happy with the increasing degree of federal-provincial collaboration in this area. The enthusiasm of the response, the high level of interest on the part of organized community groups and the private sector, the high level of focus on projects of lasting value, and the hard work of the ministerial advisory boards are combining to produce what I believe will be not only the largest but also the best program of direct job creation which has been seen in any country.
Altogether, Canada Works will provide about 348,000 man months of employment to about 77,100 participants this year. Twenty million dollars of the additional funding will go to Young Canada Works. Together with the previous allocation to this program, Young Canada Works will be using some $50 million this summer to create jobs for approximately 32,000 students.
This increase, again, is made possible by the strong public response to this program. A great number of high quality projects have been submitted and it is clear that the ministerial advisory boards have a larger shelf of sound projects from which to select.
The total funding for Canada Works and Young Canada Works for this fiscal year will thus be some $300 million. I will shortly be announcing the allocation of these funds to each constituency and asking the ministerial advisory boards to come together again if necessary to select the projects most needed by both adults and students. The summer component of this program is operated by boards of trade and chambers of commerce and provides work experience of up to nine weeks for potential school dropouts. The winter component provides young people who have left school with an opportunity for

comparable private experience leading to permanent employment.
The Job Experience Training Program is a key response to the perennial problem of the young worker who cannot get a job without relevant private sector experience, and cannot get experience without a job. Our earlier, highly successful pilot projects with the private sector have demonstrated that the program works well in the summer, and I have every confidence that it will turn out to be just as successful this winter. It is a good example of how the private sector and the federal government can co-operate, both to provide immediate employment for young people and to overcome their longer-run problems.
Although our funding increase at the moment is modest, I would like to see the Job Experience Training Program expand considerably. I hope that it may become one of the main instruments of a true partnership to reduce youth unemployment. I have received a number of interested inquiries from the private sector about how they can contribute even more to our employment strategy. If interest continues to build, and it seems practical, I will be prepared to consider a reallocation of funds from other portions of the employment strategy to help provide young people with employment and training through this program.
I should like to be able at this time to announce an increase in the availability of our funds to help provinces launch co-operative education programs. Co-operative education, which ensures that students get relevant work experience and contacts with the private sector during the course of their studies, is one of the better avenues of approach for resolving youth employment problems. Co-operative education programs are not, though, always easy to start up. They take a great deal of planning and collaboration and hard work to arrange. I hope that our further consultations with the provinces on this matter may lead to productive applications for even more than the million dollars of co-operative education projects that we would hope to assist them with this year. Again, if that proves to be the case, I will be prepared to consider a reallocation of funds in that direction.
Most of our extra funding is, appropriately, being provided for the established direct job creation programs which I have mentioned. But I also plan to reserve a small amount-about $3 million-for a new program which I hope to develop with the provinces and private industry.
For some years we have witnessed the situation where we have at the same time high youth unemployment rates and shortages of skilled tradesmen. These skills take from three to five years to produce, by a mixture of training in industry and short courses in provincial institutions. The careers they open up are both interesting and increasingly well paid. Yet despite the real attractions of these occupations, we in Canada have always had to import workers from abroad. Each year some
20,000	skilled tradesmen enter Canada to fill jobs which would otherwise go begging. At the same time our young people have
April 4, 1977

an unemployment rate which, on an annual basis, is currently about 12.8 per cent. We simply must arrange our affairs in such a way as to bring together unemployed young people and the continuing demand for skilled tradesmen.
I am determined that we will fill this gap. There are many difficulties in doing so-the long period of sometimes low wages that apprentices face; employer reluctance to face the high costs of training when their future needs for tradesmen may seem uncertain; reluctance on the part of some unions locals to accept an expansion in the number of qualified tradesmen. These problems are all understandable; what we need is a means of overcoming at least some of them. 1 will be consulting with my provincial colleagues to see whether we can together develop appropriate means of helping industry to take on more apprentices and helping Canada by having more qualified tradesmen when we need them.
Altogether, the increment of $100 million will bring the employment strategy expenditures for this year to over $450 million. The over-all pattern of these expenditures this year reflects both where we feel the immediate priorities should go and the establishment of some new initiatives which may well become the mainstays of the employment strategy in future years.
Of the total sum, some $422 millions are to be spent on one form or another of direct job creation. They will generate
600,000	man-months of employment and help to reduce our high unemployment rate without setting off another round of inflation.
Some $27 million will be utilized for increased training under the Canada Manpower Training Program and the Canada Manpower Industrial Training Program. The remainder will go to increase the scale of programs that help people find or keep private sector jobs, including our youth employment centre.
The employment strategy will also make a very considerable contribution to alleviating both the short and the long-term problems of youth unemployment. Over $96 million will be utilized this summer on youth-specific employment and training programs-nearly four times the $24 million of last summer. If normal ratios prevail, close to $250 million of our employment strategy will be used to help young people get jobs.
Through these various changes we have greatly strengthened the capacity of the employment strategy to combat unemployment this year. The total number of people who will get jobs or training through it will be over 177,000. It will reduce unemployment rates where they are highest and amongst the groups that have the highest unemployment rates. It will have an immediate and beneficial impact on the economy as a whole. It will do that without adding to inflation or pushing us beyond our means.
As I have indicated, however, the employment strategy is far more than just a series of measures designed to provide temporary jobs for those who need them. It is a co-ordinated set of measures, flexible in terms of its application, designed
The Budget-Mr. Dick progressively to attack long-run structural employment problems as well as to bring down high immediate unemployment rates. It is a strategy not just for the year 1977 but for the future as well.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Will the minister accept a question?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I noticed that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in the budget speech last Thursday evening, and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) in his speech this evening, talked about man-months of employment, instead of the customary man-years. Some time ago when I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) a question about jobs in a local customs office, she referred to those as temporary jobs and spoke in terms of man-years. Why did the minister this evening speak about man-months of employment? Does he think that if he multiplies by 12 the program will look larger than it actually is?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. The reason has to do with accuracy. Many programs, including Canada Works and Young Canada Works, are geared on a monthly rather than a yearly basis. Man-months of employment provides a more accurate description. Perhaps the hon. member noticed that I said how many jobs the program will create in one year. Surely it is simple to divide by 12. It is not a question of trying to "con" anyone; it is just a question of these programs operating on a monthly rather than on a yearly basis.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to participate in this debate, especially in view of the fiction perpetrated by the government party. Divide the
600.000	man-months of work for 177,000 Canadians by 12, and you will see that the government will provide a mere
50.000	annual jobs for the million or more unemployed, or jobs for about 5 per cent of the unemployed. I am glad the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) asked the minister to clarify the point, because it shows the government has inflated the figures.
I am sorry to note that the minister is about to leave, now that he has read his junk into the record. 1 wanted him to hear some of my comments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have been here all day listening very carefully to the addresses which have been made, and I can assure the hon. member that I will read his remarks, but whether he knows it or not there are other jobs ministers have to do besides give speeches and listen to speeches. 1 know of his interest in unemployment and particularly in youth unemployment, and I will read his remarks very carefully.

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Dick

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased. 1 hope I can be instructive and help the minister along so that the band-aid approach which has been used will not continue to be used.
The problem with the measurement of unemployment is that the rate of unemployment in Canada is measured as the number of persons in the labour force who do not have jobs. But it is not enough just to be of working age to be a member of the labour force. A person must also have a job or be looking for a job. Thus, if the number of people of working age who are looking for jobs decreases, the unemployment rate will decrease, even though the number of unemployed and the number of people of working age remain constant. This is the reason the unemployment rate may not present a true picture.
For example, in 1975 of the 418,000 possible new workers only three quarters actually joined the labour force, either had jobs or were looking for jobs. In 1976 people were so discouraged that only about one third of the possible new workers, 383,000, entered the labour force. That illustrates the problem. Even though the working age population has not grown as fast as in previous years, if the participation rate among the new working age population had remained at its 1975 level of three quarters, there would have been an extra
145,000	Canadians counted as unemployed members of the labour force. This would have made Canada's unemployment rate for the month of February, 1977, 8.8 per cent rather than 7.5 per cent. The crunch is that if people get tired of looking for jobs because there are none to be found and, as a consequence, they drop out of the labour force, the unemployment rate will no longer reflect the true labour problem. I think it is important that we bear that in mind because the figures have been deflated considerably from what they in fact really ought to be.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) indicated how many new jobs he is going to create and some of the wonderful things he is going to do. At the same time in tonight's paper it is reported that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) indicates that the budget will not help the jobless. In another newspaper the Minister of Finance is reported to have said he is powerless to reduce the jobless rate. How can these statements reflect what is really happening if the Minister of Manpower and Immigration says he is going to create so many new jobs? One of the ministers has to be wrong. I think perhaps the Minister of Finance is more accurate, especially when we find out that instead of 177,000 new jobs-if we divide by 12 the 600,000 man-months-we would actually get only 50,000 new jobs.
One of the things which is of great concern to me is that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration said early in his remarks that the labour force is growing faster than the number of job opportunities and that we have an "unusually high" unemployment rate this winter. By that I assume the minister means he did not know this would happen. He seems to indicate this problem is temporary.
I note also on page five of the budget that the Minister of Finance said, and I quote:
[Mr. Cullen.)
The most disturbing element in our performance has been the recent increase in unemployment. I am particularly troubled by the unemployment among the young people of this country.
We have given a high priority to direct job creation programs, especially for young people ...
Mr. Speaker, it has been said time and again by the Minister of Finance and by previous ministers of finance that unemployment in our country is of a "temporary" nature, "unusually high" or that there have been "recent" increases.
I would like to speak for the young people of this country. They could perhaps be referred to as being "The forgotten Canadians" by the government. That is not a recent development. The figures I want to give are not temporary figures or figures which are just a little out of the ordinary. In December of 1973 unemployment among people between 14 and 24 years of age was 9.7 per cent. That is a very high figure. In December of 1974 the figure was 10.6 per cent. That was an increase, even back in those days. In December of 1975 the figure increased again to 12.5 per cent. In December of 1976 the figure went up to 13.4 per cent, and in January, 1977, the figure went up to 15.2 per cent. Finally, the actual unemployment rate for young people in February was 16.1 per cent, a further increase.
How can the government talk about an "unusually high" rate of unemployment? How can it talk about a "temporary" situation or about a "recent" increase? If the government would only read its own figures it would realize that this problem has been growing for five years. Our present problem was predictable. The government seems to ignore this and tries to pretend that this is a temporary problem. It always appears to be temporary to this government because it wants to deal only with today; it does not like looking into the future.
The government has announced some youth employment programs for this year, and I think it should be borne in mind the relationship of these programs to what has happened in the past. In 1973 the federal government spent $85.4 million to create 67,000 jobs for youth. Again in 1974 the government spent $85.4 million to create some 67,000 jobs for youth. In 1975 that figure was decreased, although unemployment among youth was increasing. It was decreased to $67 million to create some 37,000 jobs for the young people of this country. In 1976, the year the government really hit rock bottom, it announced in its budget that it would spend $60 million. However, the government did not spent $60 million. In fact the minister has confirmed the figure I have. In his speech today he said that in 1976 the government spent $24 million to create 12,000 jobs. The unfortunate thing is that the minister now boasts that he has almost quadrupled the figure for this year and that he is going to spend some $96 million to try to create, as he said, 177,000 jobs.
How an increase from $85.4 million in 1973-74, which was to create only 67,000 jobs, to $96 million to create 177,000 jobs can be done is beyond my mathematics. I presume it is beyond the mathematics of most people when they consider the minimum wage in this country. The fact is that back in 1973-74 the government was spending $85 million to create work for youth and that only now is it getting back to the same
April 4, 1977

range, and that is not really the same level of spending when we take inflation into account. Until this budget came down the total figure the government had in mind for this year was $55 million to create 33,000 jobs.
Since the government realized that unemployment among youth is completely out of hand because of its irresponsible management of the economy, it has turned around and put together a whole bunch of new programs or added to other existing programs. We find that it is going to add another $50 million for the Canada Works Program and another $20 million for the Young Canada Works Program. On April 4 it announced another $20 million to be put in place for people to start work in four weeks' time. That is what I call unplanned job creation.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration went through a list of another $3.5 million here, $10 million there, $6.4 million added on to old programs-these are sizeable amounts but they will not be used efficiently because there is not enough time to get things into place. The government is coming in with too little too late. It is not even back to the real spending figures it used in 1973-74 to help the youth of this country, and yet this year we have the highest rate of unemployment among youth in the history of the country.
The government tries to make us believe that it is really interested in youth and really wants to help youth, but every time it announces a program it is only a few weeks before youth is supposed to be involved. Young people who are serious about what they want to do this coming summer should have taken action last November. Application forms for Young Canada Works were issued in January but, Mr. Speaker, they had to be returned by February 26. That was not a lot of time to do any planning. The applications should have been out last November and there should have been an advertising program then.
Another two youth-oriented programs have been announced in the last two weeks but they will not be of any benefit to our youth for this summer. The Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) announced a Canada student exchange program but he did not know how much money would be available for it. He said he hoped about 30,000 young people would take advantage of it but he did not give figures on how much they were going to get. He said travel costs from region to region would be paid and that students would be matched through a computer. But again, applications would not be available until June, he said. After that the matching will be done, so I do not know how many young people will still be around. By that time they may have found jobs or have started back to school. No wonder the minister did not put a monetary figure on the program. He will have to carry it through to next year to get anything out of it.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) also announced a new program. Mr. Speaker, that Katimavik program was announced in the throne speech. Another $8 million will be earmarked for 1,000 young people in 33 job locations. But, Mr. Speaker, they do not know where those 33
The Budget-Mr. Dick
places will be this summer. The minister said he hopes to have the program in place by September, that the young people will be paid $1 per day, and $3 per day will be saved for them and paid at the end of the program. I hope he does not intend to employ anyone between the ages of 17 and 22 who smokes or drinks pop because that allotment would not cover a packet of cigarettes and a coke every day. They will not be able to afford to go to a movie, either. I wonder how they can introduce that as a job program or an employment strategy. I wonder, too, how many minimum wage laws this breaks. I do not think anybody is allowed to work for $1 a day under the minimum wage laws.
These programs have not been well thought out; they are just designed to catch the notice of the press. Youth will not benefit, and unemployment will probably be as high this year as it has been for the last four years.
Since 1953 the government has issued a youth questionnaire each summer relating to student unemployment. The labour force survey used in May, 1975, leads off with the question: was this person a full-time student in March of this year? Mr. Speaker, that is normally a month when people who are students are at school. Next the questionnaire asks: what does this person expect to be doing in the fall? They must answer whether they are going back to school. Then the questionnaire goes into more detail about what sort of educational institution they plan to attend, what they expect to be doing in the fall, and what is the main reason they will not be full-time students in the fall. Student unemployment figures can be assessed as a result of this survey.
Last year the government did not want to show the figures because they would disclose how high student unemployment was. It got rid of that survey and introduced another couple of questions such as: last week was so-and-so enrolled in school, college or university, or, was so-and-so enrolled as a full-time or part-time student, and in what kind of school? If that questionnaire went out in the second week in August of course it would show they were not at university because universities are not open during the first week in August, so a person would not be a student under the criteria of the questionnaire. That is the sneaky way the government tried to deceive young people going to universities. I hope the government will reinstitute the student surveys this summer so that it will be able to project what is going on with student unemployment from one year to another as it had from 1953 until this survey it came out with last year.
It is sad that the government has sunk so low that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) advised students at the University of Toronto that if they are dissatisfied with job opportunities in Canada, they should go to another country. Not all our young people come from families of relative wealth who can afford to send them overseas to hitch-hike around the world as the Prime Minister was fortunate enough to do. Some of the young people and students in this country have to work for a living, through economic necessity. They cannot afford to spend eight or ten years bumming around the world, much as they would enjoy it. They sometimes have to work to pay back

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Dick
university loans, to pay their parents back, or to help the second, third or fourth child in the family.
By and large the young people of Canada want to work. They want a meaningful job in society and they want to have a positive input to help the country prosper and expand. Instead they get a slap in the face. The government does not help with its band-aid approaches.
Here is an example of government advertising for one of the Young Canada Works programs. In part it reads as follows:
The students will work on projects of community benefit that will enable them to test their career aspirations.
In the next paragraph we are told the projects will last between six weeks and 14 weeks. In that relatively short period of time I hope they can find what their career aspirations are going to be and I hope they will get real understanding, at the minimum wage, of the type of work they would like to do. It is a laugh, I cannot say anything more.
The government is deceitful in its treatment of the youth, the "forgotten Canadian," in this mass unemployment which we have. We have a Minister of Finance who says it is beyond his capacity to alleviate the problem. It is the government which created the problem, but now it cannot solve it. It seems that it is just not interested in the young people of this country who want to contribute so much. Young Canadians are the most overlooked, snubbed, and neglected segment of this society. They would have to be classified as the "ignored" or "forgotten Canadians". If nothing else made this self-evident, the Prime Minister's talk to the Toronto university students surely brought this out.
Back in 1972 the Prime Minister failed to take young people's problems seriously. In an article in the Gazette of February 29, 1972, he said that in periods when the economy is slack and jobs are not plentiful, the gap between a pay cheque and an unemployment insurance cheque could be filled by schemes similar to the government's Local Initiatives Program and Opportunities for Youth Program. The idea, he said, is to find something for these people to do-like assistance to the aged, baby-sitting, or teaching languages. Now his government is suggesting programs like Young Canada Works as a stop-gap-but I would like to point out that his band-aid approach has lasted five years already. It is absolutely intolerable to think that this ad hocery should continue.
The report on youth and employment by the Canadian Council on Social Development says that there will be a continued growth of population for those aged 20 to 24 until well into the 1980's. It is well past the time that the government realized that the youth unemployment situation could become chronic unless long-range plans are implemented immediately.
Young Canadians, aged 15 to 24, represent approximately 26 per cent of our total population and about 24 per cent of the total employed labour force, and yet they represent about 46 per cent of the total unemployed labour force as of Febru-

ary of this year. For these young people the future is bleak. As the leader of our party stated a few days ago:
Young Canadians-to whom Mr. Trudeau says: 'If you want a job leave the country'-cannot be expected to develop a work ethic until there is work to have ethics about.
If the Prime Minister were at all capable of understanding how insecure and uncertain Canadians are feeling, he would have never made such ridiculous statements to the Toronto university students. Instead of attempting to understand their feelings-and, I might add, justifiable feelings-of fear over their future prospects, the Prime Minister has treated these people with complete disrespect and contempt. He said:
We're not going to put millions into subsidization of university graduates because they have a bleak view of the future.
Yet never for one moment did he stop to consider why young people just might consider their future so bleak.
A Statistics Canada report on the 1974 university graduates showed that four months after graduation 11.4 per cent of the students were still unemployed and a further 17 per cent were underemployed. A year later, of this same group of students, 7.2 per cent were still unemployed and a further 11 per cent were underemployed, yet the unemployment rate for 1974 was an over-all 6.1 per cent, and only 4.1 per cent for those 25 years of age and over. So, when the Prime Minister says to the Toronto university students:
There's no case for university graduates. They're the ones who get the jobs,
I suggest, in view of the aforestated statistics, that he is simply talking off the top of his head and without any knowledge or commitment.
Youth unemployment has been, and will continue to be, a long-term problem, and not merely a temporary surplus as the Minister of Manpower and Immigration would like us to believe.
The Canadian Council on Social Development dismisses this temporary surplus myth by saying that the 20 to 24 year old age group will continue to grow well into the 1980's. Other myths, such as that young people are over-educated, as the Prime Minister would have us believe, are also dismissed. The so-called logic of why one cannot appreciate a good job until one has experienced a series of bad jobs escapes me, because it certainly never applied to the Prime Minister. But, more important, as our young people grow older, the pattern of poor job experience today will be transmitted into the future- unemployed young people today may simply be the working poor of tomorrow. This is why some long-term planning by government is essential. It is not sufficient to view the high unemployment of our youth as temporary and to offer ridiculous temporary solutions like Young Canada Works, or any other band-aid solutions which last a matter of weeks and then leave the person without a job again.
These young Canadians-the generation popularly known as the "post war baby boom"-have been subjected to a series of "temporary solutions"-from "temporary" classrooms for a school system that could not absorb them all, to being "temporarily" kept off the labour market by the need for a higher
April 4, 1977

education philosophy, and now they are facing a labour market which cannot absorb them, and the federal government says they are a "temporary" surplus and offers them "temporary" stop-gap solutions. If a number of young people have become discouraged and stopped searching for employment, is it any wonder at all?
As a spokesman for youth in our party 1 have had the privilege of visiting many universities and many groups of young people and I find that young people want jobs. They want to add to our country. They also want security. They want permanent, meaningful jobs. Some of them would like to get married and raise a family, others would like to buy a car. You cannot do that on "temporary", stop-gap programs which will give them employment for only six to 14 weeks or, as the Minister of Manpower and Immigration admitted himself, on a month to month basis. They do not know where they will be in the future because the government refuses to deal with the problem. The young people of this country, sad to say, are the "ignored Canadians". They are the "forgotten Canadians", forgotten by this government, and it is a sad indictment that the government will not take steps to cure the highest unemployment rate in our history for the young people of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel privileged to be able to enter this important debate. Although I have spoken on one or two throne speeches, this is a first for me on a budget. During his career in the House a member wants to engage in the whole spectrum of activities because, if he is serious, he deems it his duty to contribute all he can to national decisions and issues.
The throne speech opens a new session or a new parliament and outlines new hopes and vistas for government and national consideration. It tries to illuminate short-term as well as long-term targets. A budget speech, conversely, is in one way a pragmatic review of past expenditures. It is a moment of truth. It is also a melange, of targets missed or realized, and it makes forecasts for action both immediate and remote. It is the government's hour of confession and self-appraisal. But implicitly, an honest government and an honest minister of finance will lay bare those unforeseen events which have caused adjustments to estimates. A courageous finance minister gives the country the unvarnished truth, as has the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in this budget. Also because he is an intelligent, patriotic Canadian, with a great deal of ministerial know-how he, as he did last Thursday with the rest of us, looks at the future and charts a carefully planned course of action.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Because of obvious difficulties in the present national and international scene, and because sailing these dangerous waters demands high purpose, a clear head, and a happy ending to the voyage, his budget was an excellent compromise. It gave stimulation to the economy, and enough
The Budget-Mr. Railton
tax relief to soften our policy of restraint which, if overdone, would induce further unemployment. Budgets take six to 12 months to show results. But by the end of 1977, and the spring of 1978, the present recessionary period should be safely past. The long-term future will depend on world events, and the imaginative co-operation of all Canadians who believe that this is Canada's century.
Antedating this important budget, Canada was presented with the Parti Quebecois election last November. The government takes note of the fact, and its threat to a united and prosperous Canada. However, it is imperative to carry on as though separation will not happen. We can prevent it if we mobilize the silent majority both in Quebec and Canada as a whole. It is other factors outside Canada which have contributed to our inflation as well as to our unemployment. Turning on a tap of spending, either by increasing wages or prices, or by prodigal job creation, would be irresponsible. Parsimonious restraint on the obverse would only increase unemployment. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, before this very important budget was introduced, Canada has had to face the electoral success of the Parti Quebecois last November. This government must now pass the test of creating a united and wealthy country. However, we must go on as though separatism did not exist. By mobilizing the silent majority in Quebec and in the rest of Canada, we will be able to work together to maintain our national solidarity. Other factors outside Canada have influenced the levels of inflation and unemployment. To reach our objectives, we must not raise wages or prices, nor create overly well paid jobs which would increase unemployment. [English]
Right here I should like to say that although the previous speaker heaped contumely on the Young Canada Works program, Senator Hubert Humphrey in the United States has taken this program, and the effort of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), as an example for that country to follow and has brought a bill before the Senate along the same lines as the action taken by our own minister. I think that will serve as a rebuttal of the hon. member's remarks.
World economists and OECD surveys show that in spite of the opposition's misleading doom-and-gloom critics, Canada is still third or fourth in economic performance in the world. She has to live with the realities of a European Economic Community slowdown, the United States recession, demands from NATO for greater participation, as well as obligations to the Commonwealth; and in addition she has to meet the huge recent industrial competition of the poorly paid workers in the Third World. Canada must compete in the traditional pattern, but with great energy and imagination, as well as with true friendship.
Only a minority of Canadians realize that we possess a great land mass with many mineral resources, forests, and extensive continental shelves, along with inland water, great agricultural potential, and a good base of industrial technology. Our geo-

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Railton
graphical position poses expensive obstacles to our development. This is aggravated by our sparse population. Our cold winters increase costs of home and plant and public building heating, so our industries must add to energy costs of manufacturing the costs of our severe winters.
We suffer by comparison with Japan, the United Kingdom, Europe generally, and our more southern neighbours, the United States, as regards transportation cost. It is so far from one region to another in Canada. In spite of a generous endowment of energy which is contained in fossil fuels, our exploration and development costs increase every few hundred miles further north. For example, a gas well in the Beaufort Sea last year cost $30 million to drill. The minister can state unequivocally that there is no cheap energy anywhere, after surveying our gas, oil, coal, atomic energy and renewable energy resources. Conservation is a must. Reduced demand goes with it. World oil prices will soon rise, and now we have hard decisions to make about development of our energy resources. Priorities are emerging, and the timing of the phases of these developments will depend on our decisions regarding industrial development, regionalization of industry, and to a great extent on our success in settling disputes between labour and industry.
All these factors or obstacles have not prevented the government from upgrading our country's living standard to the world's highest; from providing the best social security system anywhere as regards health, family needs, senior citizens, and veterans coverage. Unionized labour is better paid in Canada than anywhere else. The wage level is still above the United States average. Canada, too, has provided multicultural benefits to her ethnic groups. She has made a very costly attempt through her bilingual policy to preserve Canadian unity and to prevent the disappearance of this nation which has so much to offer her own citizens as well as the causes of world peace and the general acceptance of the principle of the interdependence of nations.
This discussion leads us inevitably to review our industrial and export picture. A recent report from the Science Council of Canada reveals the trend since World War II. Under C. D. Howe, Canada became fully industrialized for war production. In the succeeding 15 years, production and export continued merrily, and prosperity increased by leaps and bounds. Even in the 1960's industrial expansion and resource development continued without any difficulty because the industrial nations, of which we were one, supplied the whole world with manufactured commodities and a lot of its food. Canada had a positive trade balance. She exported raw materials, minerals and timber, and had no trouble selling agricultural and manufactured products.
In the 1970's there was an abrupt change. The Third World "low technology" manufacturing countries now began to swamp the market. In 1973, the Arab oil price bomb was dropped and energy prices were quadrupled. Though exports of our primary products continued fairly strong, our oil and

gas policy now reacted by curbing exports of these resources, and this is continuing.
Whereas we had at least some domestic markets for textiles, leather goods, bicycles and consumer electronics, these can no longer compete advantageously. Similarly, in high technology areas such as fibres, chemicals, heavy machinery, transport equipments, office machinery and appliances, a trade deficit of almost $7 billion has arisen. Even the United States worries about the ascendancy of Japan and Germany in these fields. In this budget one sees the ugly fact that we had to remove the preferential treatment accorded United Kingdom heavy machinery-and Britain is a Commonwealth colleague.
So in Canadian industry, research and development, both government and private, have declined. Productivity is comparatively poor. Our labour costs are higher than those of our immediate and remote competitors. The Canadian investment climate has become troubled. The United States economy is weaker than formerly, and our exports of manufactured commodities have shrunk. Obviously we must find ways to improve our economy and particularly our export record. It is my opinion that we should try to supply at least 60 to 70 per cent of our domestic market in order to build a strong manufacturing base. By increasing our research and development we can keep pace in technology. This technology would be all the better if it had an indigenous Canadian flavour. Our products must have excellence and they must be unique. We cannot allow mere copying of foreign models.
The Science Council of Canada, which confirms my last remarks, also lists six points in the strategy to improve Canada's industrial and export capability, and these are as follows: first, concentration on specialization and selectivity; second, judicious government intervention and support to rationalize industry in its areas of specialization. These moves would stem from assessment of Canada's domestic needs. Third, we would do well to go back to a re-evaluation of the Gray report on Canadian industry, foreign investment, and subsidiary companies. This would encourage Canadian owned and controlled private companies in these selected areas. Fourth, steps must be taken to aggregate domestic markets, and concentrate government purchasing to build efficient Canadian corporations. Fifth, nuclear and defence programs must be harnessed to the policy of Canadian industrial enhancement. Sixth, we possess unique, indigenous industries in Canada. These require pushing and intensification by furthering our own research and development and using complementary foreign technology.
Examples of Canadian indigenous technology with a high degree of excellence are our aircraft industry, our locomotives and rolling stock, both passenger and freight, our ice-breaker cargo ship, our heavy water plants, and that superlative Canadian triumph, the CANDU reactor. We have our communications satellites and communications equipment, our northern drilling and pipe line experience, and our hydro know-how. Our next push should be into the realm of renewable resource technology. This has been brought into the open by Bill C-309 standing in the name of the hon. member for
April 4, 1977

Davenport (Mr. Caccia). Ele proposes an institute for solar energy, which I support in principle.

speechtext:
The details that I have just outlined must then be taken into account and a budget produced to satisfy the multitude of Canadian needs. Our Anti-Inflation Board has performed very creditably. It has certainly modified the sharp rise in inflation. It has controlled prices as well as wages and salaries. Individuals and corporations have co-operated well.
The government has reduced its increase in expenditures from 24 per cent two years ago to 11 per cent last year, and aims at 9 per cent this year. This was an immense achievement. Its target last year had been a 17 per cent reduction. The civil service has restricted its personnel increase to one per cent annually, below the rate of population growth. Maxwell Henderson misanthropically chides the government for a 400 per cent or more increase in expenditures over the last 10 years, but he conveniently avoids saying that the gross national product has risen at a parallel rate.
High unemployment figures exist everywhere in the world, not only in Canada. We are particularly concerned, however, with the 14 per cent rate for all youth, against the 7 to 9 per cent for all women and 5 per cent for all adults. We worry that the Atlantic provinces have such a high unemployment rate, and Gaspe in Quebec as well. In the middle range are Saskatchewan, Manitoba, northern Ontario and the rest of Quebec. This aspect will, we hope, be ameliorated by introduction of a doubling of the 5 per cent investment tax credit in the Atlantic provinces and Gaspe, as well as raising it to l'h per cent in the designated central areas of Canada.
So, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance fully recognizes the need for an intensified and continued struggle against inflation, unemployment and "business doldrums". He had a very fine line to tread. It is well known that fixed expenditures such as the national debt, social security, Crown agencies, cost shared programs and agreements with the provinces and equalization payments, as well as all the other needs of the economy which I detailed, leave the minister only some 10 to 20 per cent of the total budget which can be changed.
That is why he has set himself some important goals, and they are as follows: first, to persuade us all individually and in groups to lower our expectations regarding our share of the total available national income; second, to remember the need to assist our senior citizens, the handicapped, the pensioners, the veterans and the low income group of workers. His budget has given relief to these groups. Third, to give judicious stimulus to all business, but particularly small business. Too big a dose would cause more inflation; too little would allow business stagnation. He has seen clearly the need to provide for regional disparities. He has wisely left on controls until at least next October, and maybe until 1978. Clearly it will take assurances from both organized labour and industry to accept the decontrols period with promised self-restraint, or the controls will have to remain.
The Budget-Mr. Yewchuk
It is patently foolish for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) to ask for removal of controls immediately. The former is deluded with the free market place philosophy and apparently he is deluding himself and the public. The other, with his socialistic patter, intimates that we are fighting inflation on the backs of the workers. Both men need to get down to grips with reality and be more honest with themselves.
I mentioned the criticisms of the two leaders of the opposition. I have discarded them as being quite trivial. The press has shown that most of their group understand the difficulties facing the Minister of Finance in preparing his budget. They give him credit for having the courage to see things as they really are. They congratulate him on his ability to diagnose our national ills and, as our country's adviser, to realize that major surgery is contra-indicated. The minister is competent and sensible enough to realize that careful treatment and nursing the economy along with patience and devotion will see us through the next few months and provide us with greatly improved national health within the coming year.
