subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have used that opening, Mr. Speaker, just to demonstrate that the bilingual program has been a failure!
1 want to begin by expressing great regret that the budget speech made no mention of the subject of agriculture. There was a small tax change suggested in so far as selling a farm is concerned and reinvesting the money in another farm within a certain period.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was suggested by us first.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was indeed suggested by my party before, but that does not even pretend to come to grips with the problems that are facing agriculture in this country today. Everyone knows that the problem is one of a decreasing financial viability of agriculture as a whole. Concomitant with that, we have a situation where farmers are no longer held in the high esteem that they used to be held in as producers of the country's food supplies. If we talk to some of our urban brethren we find that their treatment of farmers, on many occasions, is such that it indicates that they rate the farmer very low on the social scale. That kind of rating of the farmer is clearly reflected in the policies of this government, and was certainly reflected in the absence of mention of farmers in the

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Yewchuk
budget speech. In other words, the government seems to place the farmers so low on the social scale that they do not even deserve a mention in the budget speech, which should have offered solutions to the many problems farmers are facing all across Canada.
We have seen, over the past decade, and even before that, a fairly steady stream of people from the rural areas into the cities. These people were farmers who, after having given it the good old college try, concluded that there was just no way to continue operating the family farm, gave it up in total despair and disgust, and went to the city to look for better things.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some of us went into politics.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is right, some of them went into politics and indeed accompany us in this House at this particular time. We all know that farmers could produce a lot more food for the starving people of the world if they were encouraged and if they were guaranteed or assured of some kind of reasonable return for their labour and investment. There has, by no means, been any such assurance. Therefore, they are not producing to resolve the food shortage problem that the world faces today.
As a result of the difficulty in economic viability of farming operations, we have seen a couple of things which are of concern to me. One of them is that the age of the average farmer is becoming fairly high. In other words, very few young farmers are beginning in this business. If they did, they would only be doing it for love of the lifestyle which a farmer enjoys, rather than with any prospect or any hope of making a reasonably good living doing that kind of work. The result of the aging population of the farm, from the long term point of view, could be fairly serious for the country, making it more and more dependent on imports and less and less able to produce enough food to feed its own people.
Part of the problem has been a very great lack of stability in the farm situation. There have been some small efforts made to combat this instability. One of these has been the grain stabilization program. That in itself has done very little to produce the kind of stability that is required if we are indeed to see agriculture survive.
During the course of the few minutes that I have the floor 1 want to illustrate the problem the farmer faces from the point of view of the diminishing return that he has been receiving for his investment and his labour. Comparing that to the very sharply increasing costs he must face results in an ever-increasing number of farmers just quitting because it is impossible to carry on. If we look at the consumer price index for the past five or six years, we find that it has gone up fairly substantially. In September of 1976 the consumer price of beef was down 13 per cent from a year earlier, while all items, excluding food, were up 9.3 per cent. With respect to food consumed in the home, its costs have gone down by 2 per cent, while services of various types that people buy have increased in cost by 12.3 per cent.
Those figures clearly indicate one very important fact. That is that the net income to the producer of food in this country
(Mr. Yewchuk.)
has shown a drastic decline. If we look at the figures for net income realized by farmers as a group in this country, we note that in 1974 it was $3,804 million; in 1975 it was $4,246 million; in 1976 it was $3,362 million. In spite of drastically increased costs in the period 1974-76, net farm income not only dropped to a lower level in 1976 than in 1975, but to an even lower level than it was in 1974. If you check around the country and examined the incomes of tradesmen, labourers, professional groups or business people, you will not find another group which experiences this kind of difficulty with its income. It clearly shows there are serious problems that need to be corrected.
I have some figures in terms of the investment a farmer must make. They are for Alberta, but I would think they are similar in other provinces. In 1975 the average farm in Alberta consisted of land and buildings valued at $109,000, machinery $25,000, and livestock $17,000. This is the average taking all farmers together, realizing that there are many farmers whose investment is much higher and many whose investment is much lower. The total average investment of a farmer in Alberta is $151,000.
In 1975 the net taxable income that a farmer received on that kind of an investment was $14,000. That includes income not only from his labour but also a consideration for the interest on his investment. Calculated on the basis of a return on an investment, that brings his return to 9.3 per cent. The figure for 1976 was even less, 7.6 per cent.
If the farmer liquidated his assets and made a long term deposit of the cash, his return would have been better than the 9.3 per cent or the 7.6 per cent in both of these years. He would have obtained a better return on his money had he not worked but simply sold his assets and deposited the money. The interest would have been higher than his actual income for the years 1975 and 1976.
In short, the average farmer in Alberta paid to stay in business. Not only did he get less income than if he had not worked and simply invested his money, but he received absolutely nothing for the weeks and months of work he put into the operation of his farm.
I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is not here. I would like to ask him whether he feels the policy of the government has been fair to the farmers in Alberta from the point of view of ensuring them some kind of decent income based on the number of hours they put in, as well as based on a return on their investment.
No group other than the farmer works for no financial return. He is the only one in our society today who works for no pay at all. Indeed the return he gets does not properly cover the interest on his investment.
I now wish to deal with the price the farmer gets for his product. It may help members opposite to understand the problem which they obviously have not understood this far. In 1971 he received $1.50 a bushel for his wheat. In 1972 it was $2.87 a bushel, and in 1975 $6.23 a bushel. This year it is
April 4, 1977

down to approximately $3 a bushel. In that five-year period, wheat prices came up to a reasonable figure for a very short time. They have now dropped back to $3 a bushel. These figures will be more significant when I review later the costs the farmer has to pay.
In 1971 it cost $30 per acre to produce wheat. In 1976 the figure was $88 per acre, an increase of 293 per cent. While the price of wheat between 1971 and today has roughly doubled, up by 100 per cent, the cost of producing a bushel of wheat has gone up by 293 per cent. This clearly illustrates the point 1 was trying to make in so far as costs and incomes are concerned.
Between 1969 and 1973 the average price the farmer received for his beef product was $36.28 a hundredweight. That figure takes into consideration the very high price he received in 1972 for a short period of time. In 1973 the price was $46.50 per hundredweight. Today it is about $42 or $43 per hundredweight. This shows that the price the producer of beef receives for his product is lower today than it was four years ago.
Looking at the cost of beef production, we see that it cost about 45 cents per pound of animal gain. The price the farmer receives for his product when he sells it is 43 cents for a pound of beef, even though it cost him 45 cents a pound to produce. His return is less than the cost of production. He receives no consideration for having put a lot of work into that production.
1 want to review some other costs the farmer faces. Gasoline has doubled in cost in the past four years. Binder twine doubled in that same period, and fertilizer is a little more than double in price. The cost of tractor tires has nearly doubled.
The cost of a tractor to pull a four-bottom plough cost $7,500 in 1973. This is a basic tractor without extra equipment. Today it costs $9,500, an increase of $2,000. In 1960, that same machine cost about $4,000. In 1960, the price the farmer was getting for his wheat was in the range of $1.75 a bushel, approximately the same as in 1972. The cost of fuel, equipment and materials doubled in the past four or five years while the price the farmer received for his product, whether it be grain, beef or some other product, remained essentially unchanged or, in fact, dropped a little.
I might pause here to take a further look at the question of beef. This has been an area of great difficulty for the past couple of years. Any of us who have read speeches of the Minister of Agriculture will have seen statements by him that we are producing too much beef, that the market is glutted, and that that is the reason for the low prices. I think this is very far from the truth. The truth is that Canada has not been producing enough beef on an annual basis since 1969 to meet its own needs. There has been an oversupply of beef purely because of imports from other countries, primarily Australia and New Zealand.
I happen to have figures here which clearly demonstrate that the minister has followed a deliberate policy of squeezing out of the beef business hundreds of farmers on the excuse that there is an overproduction, knowing all the while that there is
The Budget-Mr. Yewchuk
no overproduction. The minister is just trying to make room for more and more imports from other countries. In 1975, the last year for which statistics are available, beef production in this country amounted to 2,190 million pounds. We exported about 45 million pounds, leaving 2,145 million pounds of beef available from domestic sources. Total domestic consumption, on the other hand, was 2,335 million pounds of beef, or 190 million pounds more than domestic production. I think that is very significant because the beef producer has been squeezed very severely on the excuse of the Minister of Agriculture that we have too much beef, but the fact is that we have not been producing enough to meet our own needs.
We have to ask ourselves why this government, which is supposed to be responsible to the people and sensitive to their needs, has chosen to follow this destructive course in so far as the beef farmer is concerned. On examining the reasons we find that it is because we have trade agreements with Australia, for example. Australia will buy Canadian manufactured goods and in exchange we will buy their beef. The goods consist of various types of manufactured hardware from central Canada which is sold on the Australian market. Admitted, some of the beef which is imported is of poorer quality and perhaps less costly. Canadian beef production is being sacrificed in the interests of central Canada's manufacturing industry and in the interest of the urban consumer lobby, and the western farmer is being destroyed in the process. That situation is completely intolerable and must be changed forthwith.
I wanted to make some general comments because we are not dealing with just figures when we talk about farmers; we are dealing with people who have chosen to produce food as their life's work and who have chosen to live on the farm because they like that kind of lifestyle, because they love the soil, and also because they realize that for the long-term good of the country Canada must remain self-sufficient in its food production to the maximum extent possible. It is beyond me why the government fails to recognize the situation and why it seems to choose to destroy our agricultural industry and force thousands of people off the land in favour of getting some hamburger from Australia at a few cents less a pound than it would cost to produce in this country. We know that, if that trend continues, agricultural production will continue to deteriorate and in the long run Canada will become more and more dependent on offshore sources for its food supply. And if we reach that stage of dependence we can be sure food prices will become a lot steeper than they would be had we maintained our own production capability.
I am not saying that developing a good agricultural policy is an easy matter. I am not even suggesting that all farmers should be subsidized. I am simply expressing the view that we have a government in this country which has failed totally to recognize the need to develop an agricultural policy which will keep our agricultural industry viable and productive. Unless governments in this country become more attuned to the fact that farmers will not continue to work for no wages and something has to be done fairly soon, Canada will be in difficulty in so far as its food supply is concerned.

April 4, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Yewchuk
Everyone will admit that if there is anything Canada can do well, and if there is anything that Canada is suited for, it is agricultural production. We must recognize that agriculture must remain one of the key industries in this country and that the solution to the farmers' problem is not simply to drive farmers off the land but that other solutions must be found to help them stay on the land, and to guarantee them not only a decent return on their investment but also a decent wage. If that is done, the country will be healthier as a whole.
I mentioned earlier that the average income of a farmer in Alberta in the last couple of years was in the range of $11,000, $12,000 or $14,000, that is, not counting the return on his investment. If you look at that figure by itself, you will find it is similar to the income of some tradesmen such as carpenters or mechanics who make around $7 or $8 per hour. But we must remember that a mechanic, a carpenter, or other tradesmen working at that wage level do not have to invest in their jobs apart from investing the time to educate themselves. Certainly they do not have to invest the $151,000 which the farmer must invest in his land, machinery, and livestock if he is to make a go of it.
In conclusion let me say that I hope someone on the other side will take this message to the Minister of Agriculture. It is of utmost importance to recognize that there is a problem in agriculture and that it is not fair to ask the farmer to work for no wages forever. Farmers, being people who love their country, are willing to contribute to it perhaps as much or more than any other Canadian, but to ask them to work for no wages during the entire stretch of their agricultural career is not what farmers in this country deserve.
It is time efforts were made in marketing on the international scene. I am not taking a position on whether marketing boards should or should not be set up in this country. I think that is a decision which should be left to individual producer groups. However, there are many things which could be done to assist. One would be to aim for a general reduction in imports of whatever agricultural commodities are hampering our own producers. Another thing which could be done would be to provide financing for farmers at lower cost. Steps could be taken to reduce the cost of machinery and machinery parts. We know that a number of years ago the Barber commission on farm machinery was set up. That commission made a fairly large number of recommendations. As far as I know none of those recommendations has been implemented, very much to the shame of this government.
Another aspect is the question of energy on the farm. In Alberta, which produces most of the energy in this country, farmers in my constituency and other consumers in my constituency pay more for a gallon of gas than we pay here in Ottawa. Obviously something must be wrong, when we consider that Ottawa uses Alberta gasoline! Consumers in Montreal as well as consumers in Halifax and Newfoundland are subsidized, but consumers in Peace River, High Level and Lac La Biche pay at least ten cents per gallon more than consumers in

Montreal. When this matter was brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance he simply waved his hands in the air and said that the policy is not to subsidize anybody using petroleum products produced in this country.
Those are a number of suggestions which I hope the government will consider and, if it does, the farmer may indeed survive.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed listening to the last speech, which was the only one I have had the opportunity to hear during this short budget debate. Some of the comments certainly indicate the difficulties of the farm community and the difficulties we have nationally with any and all of our programs. The hon. member suggested that we take another look at import controls. Recently I was at a conference with a group of Canadians from all parts of the country. I heard no one from the west talk about free trade, so perhaps in that area the east and the west are beginning to come together.
I am usually very independent-minded and very critical of government budgets. I find things about them which I criticize very severely.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will have a heyday with this one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: However, I think this budget is about as good a budget as we could have devised, given the general conditions and the options open to the government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How can you say that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because he is honest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There has to be a trade-off when one stimulates the economy between stimulating demand and stimulating investment, and we have traditional proponents of both in this House. Normally the NDP strongly suggest increasing demand, and the Tories are usually concerned about increasing growth by increasing investment. Personally over many years I have looked upon the demand route as being the legitimate or better route, but at this particular time I am not sure. I do not think these are normal times, and since they are not normal times we have to look in many directions, not just in one.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is your government that is abnormal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When we have an inflation rate of 7 per cent and an unemployment rate of 8 per cent, we are not in normal times.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You created those problems.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have a 4 per cent growth rate. If we created those problems, why do we have the fourth lowest inflation rate of all the OECD countries? The hon. member should not tell me we created those problems. We have world-wide inflation.
April 4, 1977

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Give us the figures for other exporting nations. Do not mislead the House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: These are not normal times for the whole world, and they are not normal for this country. 1 was interested in the statement of the prime minister of Great Britain, Mr. Callaghan, who said that governments cannot delude themselves into thinking they can buy their way out of unemployment. 1 think that is what we are being asked to do, particularly by the NDP. I must say that over the years 1 have been associated with that party, and with some pride-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Confession time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-certainly in the early years because I always felt that the NDP was a progressive party which had some new ideas-perhaps a little ahead of its time-and that it was offering something to the country. It bothers me-because 1 did not leave that party in anger or as a result of any friction-that these new ideas are not forthcoming in these very complex times when problems are so very interrelated. They are dealing in these complex times with the same simple answers they had in the forties, fifties and sixties.
Let us look at the demand side of this budget. It allows the $50 per child allowance and another $100 for work expenses. An extra $100 million is to go to direct job creation. That does not seem like a great amount a money, but in this calendar year the amount of money being fed into demand is far greater than that. It comes to something like $2.4 billion which was not in the economy last year, being diverted to the economy by the government. That comes from $900 million for the indexing of income tax, $300 million for OAS, $160 million for family allowances, $250 million for the reduction in unemployment insurance, $100 million for direct job creation, and a reduction of $300 million for work expenses, and for childrens' allowance. Then there are the other job creation programs. The Canada Works Program starts in April, and that will cost another $365 million. That comes to a total of $2.4 billion. That is a sizeable amount of money going into demand. It is going into people's pockets. It is money which was not there last year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are printing it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am saying that there is an injection of money into demand. If I were the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) I would have been very happy if some of that money which had been indexed on personal income tax could be used in slightly different ways. I would like to have used $200 million of that $900 million indexed on taxation for direct job creation. To say that there is not a degree of demand in this budget or in the government's activities is to ignore that $2.4 billion, and that cannot be ignored. That is a significant amount. It is much larger than all of the other items in the budget.
The NDP has maintained all along that demand is the basic problem and that if we create more money for demand we will solve all our problems. I would like to discuss consumer
The Budget-Mr. McRae
demand. In 1973 there was a real growth in consumer demand of 6.8 per cent; in 1974, 5 per cent; in 1975, 4.9 per cent; and in 1976, 6.3 per cent. Those are very impressive figures, indicating a steady consumer demand for goods and services.
The New Democratic Party says that we need more housing starts, and there is no doubt that we do. In 1976 housing starts inceased by 18.8 per cent to 273,000 starts, the largest number in our history. To say this is not an active economy but one that is in serious trouble and needs more demand is to say that these figures do not mean anything. We had a very substantial consumer demand, growing roughly by 6 per cent per year, and in the housing field we have had the highest number of starts in our history.
I am bothered by the assumption that, simply by injecting another billion or two into the economy, the unemployment problem would be solved. This is a very complex problem with serious structural implications. I do not think any political party should advocate just throwing more money into the pot to solve the problem. I think all parties should look very carefully at the structural nature of unemployment and then try to solve the problem that exists, and not make grandiose gestures throwing billions of dollars around.
Let us analyze the unemployment problem. In the 1950's something like 60,000 young people were coming on the labour market every year, but in 1977 about 250,000 young people will come on the labour market. In that period the population has grown by about 30 per cent but there has been a 425 per cent increase in the number of young people coming on the labour market. That is a massive increase and it creates stupendous problems. Of all industrialized countries, Canada has the biggest problem with the number of young people in the population coming on the labour market each year. This situation will continue well into the 1980's, and putting more money into the pot will not solve the problem.
In 1953 in the age group between 25 and 44, 23 per cent of the women in Canada were in the labour force; in 1974 it was 47 per cent. In the age group 45 to 66, 17 per cent of women were in the labour force, but it was 37 per cent in 1974.
The participation rate is the number of people employed divided by the number of people in the country aged 15 years and over. In 1963 the participation rate in the labour force was 53.8 per cent, seasonally adjusted and today, in 1977, it is 61.3 per cent.
We all know that these factors are extremely important in solving the problem of unemployment, but there is another factor which is perhaps even more important and that is analyzing these figures by region and by age, particularly if we look at the extremes. The extremes are the province of Alberta and the province of Newfoundland. At the end of February in Newfoundland 17.4 per cent of the total population over the age of 24 were unemployed; in Alberta the figure was 4.6 per cent. Newfoundland had four times the number of people unemployed that Alberta had. In Newfoundland 12 per cent of males over age 25 were unemployed while in Alberta it was 2.9

April 4, 1977
Adjournment Debate
per cent. In the age group of 15 to 25 Newfoundland had 28.6 per cent of males unemployed, while Alberta only had 9.1 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to interpret these figures if I could but 1 see it is ten o'clock, so perhaps 1 could pick up these remarks at this point tomorrow.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-REASON FOR FAILURE OF RAIL WEST TO RECEIVE ORDERS FOR HOPPER CARS
TRANSPORT-REASON FOR FAILURE OF RAIL WEST TO RECEIVE ORDERS FOR HOPPER CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 18 the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) announced that the government had released contracts for 2,000 hopper cars worth $80 million. Every one of those cars will be made by eastern firms.
There is a west coast manufacturing company at Squamish, British Columbia, capable of making these cars, which is faced with the layoff of 260 workers. That company bid on the contract. That company is Rail West Manufacturing Company. Rail West did not get an order for a single car. According to the government, the bids were not competitive.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), whose riding is only 30 miles from the Rail West plant, said that their bid was $10,000 more per car than the average bid price of eastern manufacturers. This was completely misleading. What the minister did not say, or even try to explain, although he is a western minister and should have cared about the jobs of 260 workers, was that the differential in quoted prices declined as the number of cars ordered increased.
The minister tried to make a hero of himself by saying the government would allow a pricing differential of $5,000 per car. Rail West was offered a measly 100 cars if they could build them for $41,000 each. The offer to take 100 cars was ridiculous, and the minister knew that. One hundred cars out of a total of 2,000-is that Confederation or is it just what it seems-tokenism? It is sometimes expected from some ministers, but we are all entitled to expect something better from a British Columbia minister when jobs in our province are on the line.
The fact is that the minister said, "You can build 100 cars if you can do it for $41,000 each.'' Rail West could not do it for 100 cars, but if they had the chance to build 500 cars it could have been done for slightly less than $42,000 per car.
About $8,000 worth of component parts for each car had to be purchased by Rail West from the very eastern companies

that were bidding against Rail West. Even if eastern firms lost 500 of the 2,000 cars to Rail West, they still would have got a significant part of the business for every rail car made by Rail West. Why was this ignored? Was it deliberate? As a result of the direct intervention of the British Columbia government, the Minister of Transport verbally, but not in writing, suggested that Rail West bid for a new and different order of 300 ballast cars. Rail West can make these ballast cars competitively, without a price differential, and compete against eastern manufacturers. And each car, as in the case of hopper cars, will mean business in component parts for eastern manufacturers.
Rail West has put in a bid; the Department of Transport is considering it. It is now time for the government to come through with an order, as 264 jobs are at stake. They are western jobs, and westerners out of work are just as unemployed as anybody else in Canada. While the country is obsessed with Quebec, remember, there are grievances in the west. This is one specific grievance we want to rectify.
It is disgusting for a western company to have to beg for what is fair. It is demeaning for a western member of parliament to have to shove, push, shout and kick, just to get someone in the government to do what is right. That should not be necessary. And if Confederation is to mean anything to westerners, this sort of massive indifference to our legitimate requests has got to stop.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-REASON FOR FAILURE OF RAIL WEST TO RECEIVE ORDERS FOR HOPPER CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to debate the point the hon. member has raised concerning Rail West's failure to receive orders for hopper cars, it is appropriate to review the recent history leading up to the awarding of contracts.
Both CN and CP, which conducted negotiations on behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), issued invitations to tender on January 5, 1977, for the 2,000 hopper cars, which would include 100-ton steel cars of 4,550 cubic foot capacity; 100-ton aluminum cars of 5,000 cubic foot capacity; 70-ton steel cars of 3,800 foot capacity; and 70-ton aluminum cars of 4,100 cubic foot capacity. The invitations were issued to four firms, including Rail West Manufacturing Company of Squamish, B.C. A fifth firm, Procor Ltd., chose not to bid.
Rail West had requested and been given a copy of the hopper car specifications several months earlier. On January 10, 1977, officials from Rail West met with the minister's officials, originally to request an extension of the January 17 deadline, but discussions drew out the fact that such an extension would not enable Rail West to improve their bid substantially. In light of this Rail West agreed to put in a bid on the date specified.

Mr. Speaker, we did look favourably upon Rail West's bid. In fact, we invited the company to share in the construction of a number of hopper cars when 2,000 of them were ordered previously. Even taking into account the difference in the cost
April 4, 1977

of steel in that area as compared with other areas, the price asked by Rail West was decidedly much higher than that of the other companies. The price we offered exceeded even that difference, and even then Rail West could not build the cars and could not commit itself to building 100 of them. In other words. Rail West's bid was considered in a very favourable light and it is unfair to raise doubts about the evolution of the situation and to insinuate that all factors were not taken into consideration in the basic study the government made of this important initiative, namely to build 2,000 hopper cars.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government, the Department of Transport and the provincial government are fully aware of the importance of the situation and its repercussions on the 260 persons concerned. That is why we are still having consultations with Mr. Phillips of Rail West.

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-PROPOSED NEW INSTITUTION FOR MANITOBA-POSSIBILITY OF SITE AT CHURCHILL OR LYNN LAKE
PENITENTIARIES-PROPOSED NEW INSTITUTION FOR MANITOBA-POSSIBILITY OF SITE AT CHURCHILL OR LYNN LAKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I want to speak on the maximum security penitentiary proposed for Manitoba. Recently the minister announced that a super maximum security prison would be built in Manitoba. Many locations in Manitoba have been considered, but I feel that the northern part of the province, where the unemployment rate is almost 20 per cent, has been overlooked. Since 45 per cent of the inmates of the maximum security prison at Stony Mountain, B.C., are of Indian ancestry, I feel the government ought to consider building the maximum security prison in northern Manitoba. I will not say in which community the prison should be built. T merely say that since 45 per cent of the inmates would come from northern Manitoba, the government should consider seriously building the prison in that part of the province.
The proposed super maximum security penitentiary would hold between 185 and 200 inmates and employ roughly 200 persons as correctional officers, guards, trades instructors, and in administrative, managerial, and other capacities. The annual payroll would be approximately $3 million, and the local buying would be in excess of $500,000, plus the local buying that would be done through wholesale houses and so on.
I really believe the northern part of the provinces would be an acceptable area in which to place a maximum security prison. We have very limited access by road and rail. Also, the inmates would have an opportunity of seeing their families because in many cases where families may have to travel from northern Manitoba to Stony Mountain they do not have sufficient funds to make that long journey.
Establishment of a maximum security penitentiary in northern Manitoba would benefit the local community concerned, and I should like to cite several such communities. Churchill is one of them. The federal government moved into Churchill in 1946 and established an armed forces training centre. In recent years the operation was transferred elsewhere and the
Adjournment Debate
fort demolished, as a result of which the town lost some $250,000 in taxes. Recently, in a cost-shared project between the province and the federal government, some $30 million was spent to rebuild the town, and now the town is faced with an ever-rising tax debt for the simple reason that the old army fort was demolished. What is needed in Churchill is some development to inject more tax dollars into the community. At the present time the only employment available there is working for the port.
Another community I could cite is the mining community of Lynn Lake. At one time this community had a population in excess of $3,000, but the mine closed down and the tax base today is very limited. At the present time Lynn Lake is being supported by the province of Manitoba. Lynn Lake has a good rail service and there is a good highway into the community. It would make an excellent location for a maximum security prison.
Another location I might mention is The Pas, Manitoba, where within the last four years the federal government has financed a shopping centre to the tune of about $81/2 million. At the present time the shopping centre is only half full of operating stores: the town is really in need of extra development and perhaps a prison could be located there. This community also has good access by rail, road, and air.
Again, I ask the minister to give sympathetic thought to locating a prison in northern Manitoba. As I say, the inmates would have an opportunity of visiting their families, especially since statistics show that 45 per cent of those in maximum security in Manitoba are of Indian ancestry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rod Blaker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-PROPOSED NEW INSTITUTION FOR MANITOBA-POSSIBILITY OF SITE AT CHURCHILL OR LYNN LAKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in this discussion on behalf of an absent Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) and his parliamentary secretary. I do hope the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) will accept the remarks I make in the absence of the Solicitor General.
The recommendations made by the hon. member are most completely accepted and well understood. The comments I make are with respect to whether or not some consideration can be give to a penitentiary service north of Churchill or whether, alternatively, there ought to be some consideration given to a penitentiary service in the Winnipeg area.
I understand that the considerations at the present time are these. In the prairie region there is demand for construction of a maximum security institution to accommodate approximately 200 inmates. The criteria recommended by the Canadian Criminology and Corrections Association, which criteria are accepted by the Canadian Penitentiary Service for guidance, require that a penal institution must be located as close as possible to the point of origin of the inmate to be incarcerated so as to allow for the maintenance of close and sound family relationships. Furthermore, access to the services of professionals such as medical doctors, psychiatrists, psychologists and social workers and so on, must be reasonably available. In

April 4, 1977
Adjournment Debate
addition, a reasonable source of manpower, such as people who might service the penitentiary and be of assistance to penitentiary programs, must be available.
The problem is that the inmates mostly originate from the general area of Winnipeg rather than from any other location in the province, and so the penitentiary service, in conjunction with the Department of Public Works, is concentrating on efforts to determine whether or not there would be some benefit in having a penitentiary further north in such areas as those mentioned by the hon. member, for example Churchill or Lynn Lake, or whether it is more desirable to have a penitentiary closer to Winnipeg.
Statistics seem to indicate that most inmates may require services closer to Winnipeg. On the other hand one questions whether the people of Winnipeg want a penitentiary close to their community or whether or not they would prefer it further north, as I have described. Perhaps the hon. member would be interested to know that as yet no decision on the part of people in the Winnipeg area as to whether or not they want a penitentiary in their community has been reached. It is really a matter of the local population deciding where they want the penitentiary.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-PROVISION OF BOXCARS FOR SHIPMENT OF POTATOES-GOVERNMENT ACTION
TRANSPORT-PROVISION OF BOXCARS FOR SHIPMENT OF POTATOES-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want this evening to present to the government and the Parliamenary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Roy) the plight of potato growers in eastern Canada. This is not a new matter, as the parliamentary secretary well knows. In fact I have raised it repeatedly since last fall. The transportation problems presently being encountered by potato producers in eastern Canada are certainly not new to them.
A week ago Friday, on March 25, I was attempting to gain from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) three answers. First of all I asked him whether he had seen a copy of the report of the Prince Edward Island Potato Marketing Board indicating the crisis on the horizon regarding the supply of railway cars to move potatoes in the next shipping season and the problems being experienced even now. Secondly, I asked whether the minister had completed his own studies. These are studies he has mentioned over the past few months but which have never been presented to the House or to my knowledge been completed. Indeed the more one looks at the studies that have been carried on by various federal departments, one finds a proliferation of them in the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and the Department of Transport, with very little, if any, co-ordination. The replacement of effective action by studies is certainly unacceptable and will be no answer to the potato producers of eastern Canada. Thirdly, because there is a meeting scheduled shortly between the provincial minister of industry and the

Minister of Transport, I asked him if he was prepared to give a definite answer at that time.
The minister of industry, the Hon. John Maloney, indicated in the provincial legislature two or three weeks ago that he recommended that some 1,800 reefers be provided. He sent this recommendation to the Minister of Transport. He will meet with him shortly to see if this decision can be confirmed.
Instead of solutions we are getting half answers, and seemingly half-hearted consideration of the problem itself. I understand there is a proposal presently being considered by the Canadian National Railways which would replace the present refrigerator cars with cars of a similar nature, some 20 or 25 years old, that are presently for sale in the United States from the Boston, Maine and Bangor railroads. They would require extensive overhauls-even with the short term life span of these particular railroad vehicles. I understand the only reason the American railways are disposing of them is because they are in such a decrepit condition that there is no self-respecting railroad in the United States that would consider operating this kind of deteriorated and soon to be inoperable equipment. Like the present reefer cars, the circulation equipment in them does not function when a car is stopped, and as a result there is very serious spoilage.
In checking with a group of producers just the other day, I was shocked to discover spoilage increases have gone up quite considerably this year because of inoperable equipment. One shipper from New Brunswick experienced with a 17-car order a complete freeze-up in which all that particular order was frozen. Another shipper in Prince Edward Island said that last year they had something like 46 frost claims to Toronto and Montreal. So far this year-and they are still not through the shipping season-they have already experienced 58 freeze-ups.
With that kind of situation it is obvious that getting used equipment from American railroads would be totally inadequate. The CNR has done some of its well-known calculations by dividing the amount of potatoes to be shipped by the size of the railroad cars and simply assuming that these will be fully loaded and shipped on a round the clock basis. These are mathematical equations which do not take into account the present marketing situation. They assume balanced shipments and that when a car is available it will be immediately loaded.
I think the railroad term is "demand loading". This would require a drastic change in our marketing system with warehousing and packaging being done at destination points, giving producers less control over their industry and obviously exploiting numbers of jobs in Prince Edward Island. This will certainly be a kind of regional development in reverse.
Obviously the rail lines in Prince Edward Island are incapable of handling the very heavy cars, 110,000 pounds capacity. The advice the Canadian National Railways have given the Minister of Transport to date unfortunately has been unrealistic with respect to the marketing needs and requirements of producers in eastern Canada. I am disappointed at the heavy reliance of the Minister of Transport on only one source of information, which seems to be the railroad in this instance, seemingly ignoring the representation made on both sides of
April 4, 1977

this House from those of us who represent the potato growing areas-members like the hon. member for Madawaska-Vic-toria (Mr. Corbin), myself, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), and others. There is also the situation with respect to his ignoring the provincial governments of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. I just wonder at the minister's audacity in ignoring those who are directly and specifically representing the marketing boards and those specifically involved in this area.
We need immediately an order for new railroad equipment, insulated boxcars capable of handling the kind of cargo that will be exported to central Canadian markets. It will also have a turn-around value in terms of bringing consumer products into eastern Canada. This has made sense for a long time.
The design for these new vehicles is already available. The order could be placed immediately. There are some 400 cars presently in existence which could be made available to growers in eastern Canada. In addition, over the next two to five years we will need 800 more cars. Obviously 400 should be ordered immediately and another 400 ordered at a very early date, perhaps with some design modification as a result of experience in using these new cars.
With the stand of the federal government at the moment, we have a double standard. As was mentioned in the earlier question by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), the government recently ordered 2,000 more hopper cars. This means some 8,000 cars are provided by the federal government to western grain shippers. In eastern Canada we have not as yet had one car either ordered or provided by the federal government for the potato producers of eastern Canada. That is a serious anomaly which I hope the Minister of Transport will very soon rectify.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-PROVISION OF BOXCARS FOR SHIPMENT OF POTATOES-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I have the pleasure of debating a matter of obvious concern to the member opposite and to other members from the maritime region, that of the adequate provision of equipment to ensure efficient movement of potatoes from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
Adjournment Debate
Potato distribution is a topic that received extensive examination for at least a decade without the implementation of substantial changes. In most instances it was judged that the present system of using old reefer cars provided the most acceptable system as far as the level of freight rates was concerned. However, it can be said that the total potato distribution system has never been thoroughly examined. There is a lack of definition, of the system requirements for storage, palletization, temperature control, and service to distribute potatoes to their different markets in a cost-effective manner. There is a need to develop long term forecasts of potato production and consumption by provinces, and to determine the desirable improvements to the present distribution system to market potato products in a cost-effective manner.
Transport Canada, along with the federal Departments of Agriculture, Industry, Trade and Commerce and DREE, is continuing to support the efforts of the various parties involved in the search and testing of up-to-date systems to transport potatoes economically.
The suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) that maybe some new reefer cars should be purchased for the use of eastern potato shippers is being reviewed by Transport Canada, Agriculture Canada, Industry, Trade and Commerce and DREE officials. All concerned federal departments are in support of the minister's intent to help the potato industry. A report with recommendations has been submitted to the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). A meeting of Agriculture Canada and Transport Canada senior officials is scheduled for April 12, 1977, to plan the next step further to the report's recommendations.
The government shares the hon. member's concern that attention be paid to the timing. On this point may 1 repeat assurances given in the House on February 10 by the minister, in response to the member's question on this subject, that he and the Prince Edward Island premier and minister of transport, have agreed to be very conscious of the timetable in looking at questions such as facilities as well as equipment.
